strength: It catches all three signals in my data. It relaunches 'Dad's razor vs mine' with new cuts, splits out women 25 to 34 instead of killing the ad set, and cuts the Starter Kit as a COD trap (₹271 break-even against a ₹463 cost). The 14-day split adds to exactly ₹5,60,000, and the ASC ladder sums correctly.
mistake: It plans ₹2,80,000 for ASC and scales DPA 20% while ASC sits above its own safe line and DPA runs at 5.2 frequency. The ₹65,000 'cost of pausing the video' is stated as fact, but it is a projection.
to10: Add a store-count forecast for the plan's profit, and make the ASC and DPA scaling depend explicitly on the UTM-adjusted line rather than on Meta's count.

strength: It gives the most honest money picture: store-count profit for each ad set, a forecast of what the plan does to the loss, and a smart geo holdout that tests whether retargeting is real lift.
mistake: It contradicts itself. Retargeting is called 'cut' in the table and 'cut by half' in the notes, budgeted at ₹2,000 a day and then run at ₹1,000 a day in the holdout. The UGC 'hold' is actually a raise to ₹4,000 a day. The 86% prospecting attribution is a guessed midpoint, and the calendar dates are invented.
to10: Make retargeting and UGC consistent between the table, the notes and the holdout, test 2 or 3 cuts of the creator hook, and justify the attribution split instead of picking a midpoint.

strength: Every rule is tied to my own numbers: the $38.46 break-even, the 4-second watch-time cut drawn from our organic hits and misses, and hooks written in Maria's and Tasha's exact words.
mistake: Spend can't start until day 4. The new on-feet creators (warehouse, teacher, line cook) don't arrive until the later rounds. The day 14 to 20 release read leans partly on TikTok-reported cost.
to10: A one-paragraph creator brief for 6 to 10 new on-feet workers, ready for day 1 outreach so new rights are secured well before the March licences end.

strength: A thorough, practical set-up list (event-ID dedup, domain check, comment moderation, Day -2 upload) plus a clear test/scale split. It also requires winners that don't sit on licensed posts before the March expiry.
mistake: The hooks use less of my customers' real words and Tasha's quotes go unused. The day-30 '790 first orders' bar assumes $38 across all spend, which clashes with judging cost on days 15 to 30 only. Smart+ scaling from day 8 is early.
to10: Write hooks from Maria's and Tasha's quotes, and make the day-30 targets consistent with each other, using two independent reads agreeing on cost per new customer.

strength: It turns all three data signals (quiet wheels, women 25 to 40 at ₹1,058, work flyers skipping the belt) into concepts, puts all three in the first three to make, and sets a sensible test budget of 15 purchases per concept, about ₹63,000 in total.
mistake: Concepts 2, 6 and 8 are statics. Concept 6 is big type on a clean colour, which sits too close to the same-looking product-on-colour style I said is flat.
to10: Replace one or two of the statics with a different format, such as a creator or UGC piece, and trim the primary text to fewer, shorter lines for grade 7.

strength: The primary text is short and calm and sounds like us, for example 'Land. Roll. Leave.' It picks the same right three concepts, keeps a control ad running, and checks its numbers: 26% of purchases for women, ₹292 a trip, about 63 more purchases.
mistake: It puts 'quiet wheels' and 'rolls quiet' into brand copy in concepts 5 and 8, a claim beyond the approved specs. Its kill rule of about ₹4,500 per concept is too thin to judge cost per purchase.
to10: Keep 'quiet' only inside buyers' own review quotes, raise the test budget to a meaningful number of purchases, and rank the cheaper women concept above the belt concept.

strength: Three distinct angles (blind test, 3 pm desk swap, game-day family) with hooks taken from real comments, and openings ordered by our cost-per-purchase data, so the label never leads.
mistake: Only Script 2 answers the $3-a-can objection. The other two state the price but never defend it, though price is 15% of comments.
to10: Handle price inside every script, add deliverables, usage rights and a test budget with cut and scale thresholds, so I can send it to creators and run it without extra planning.

strength: Production-ready package: the three angles tie to cost per purchase and comment shares, price is answered in every script ('12 afternoons for me'), and it covers disclosure, safe zones, rights, timelines and a test budget with cut and scale rules.
mistake: The spoken disclosure lands mid-scene, most awkwardly during the blind sip in Script 1, and stacks too many words into the 3-10 s window of Script 2. It also runs a little over the word limit.
to10: Move the spoken 'Olipop paid me' to a natural beat after the reveal, and trim Script 2's early lines so they fit the timing.

strength: It brings back the paused ₹210 front-of-pack winner in new words. It leads with untested taste and price lines in Aditya's and Priya's own words. The test plan has a control, a budget sized to the purchases each cell needs, cut rules and a fatigue rule.
mistake: The 4 pm samosa line and the gym line sit on the bench instead of in the first four. One of them could have replaced the near-control sugar rewrite (ad D).
to10: Pair the price-first ad with the 4 pm desk moment, so the launch set also tests Priya's habit angle against transparency and taste.

strength: It reads the data sharply: transparency is tired, not broken; taste is the unused proof; price is the objection. The legal backups for review quotes are a thoughtful touch.
mistake: Nearly every primary text repeats '12 g protein, no added sugar', and P1 and P5 are the same transparency idea. That is the 'six versions of one line' problem I asked to avoid, and there is no real 4 pm snack text.
to10: Make the six texts truly distinct, with a real 4 pm angle and less protein-plus-sugar repetition, and add a control cell and a budget that tells me when results are readable.

strength: It handles the trade-offs honestly and puts the break-in note above the fold. The 'What to know before you buy' block and the 'snug, ease in over about a week' bullet go straight at the two biggest return causes.
mistake: Customer-facing copy says the hidden pocket takes 'one more flat note', which is an invented capacity on the exact cash question we are trying to stop overstating. The SEO title also runs slightly past 60 characters.
to10: Drop the extra-note claim, use Tom's 'brick in my back pocket' phrase, and put the first-week break-in note in the line under the button.

strength: It treats about 10 flat notes as the total, hidden pocket included, so the page never overstates cash. It also uses the customer's own 'brick in your back pocket' line, gives inch conversions for US buyers, and checks the SEO lengths.
mistake: The break-in expectation sits in the description, what-fits section and FAQ but not in a bullet or the under-button line, so a fast buyer can still miss it. The 10 to 11 mm figure for 6 or 7 cards is interpolated rather than given in the data.
to10: Add 'Slots start snug and settle in about a week' to the card bullet or under the button, and measure lift against a holdout rather than a before-and-after comparison.

strength: Email 2 is split three ways by quiz answer, and the sunscreen email answers white cast, stickiness and makeup using the dusky-skin review as proof.
mistake: Email 5 pushes one 3-step routine to everyone. It includes salicylic wash morning and night, and it goes to the dry, sensitive and beginner readers it told earlier to avoid acids. That undoes the personalisation and the start-slow promise.
to10: Make the final email's routine match each quiz answer, with one active plus sunscreen, and add a holdout and a rupee value for the lift.

strength: Personalisation by quiz answer runs through the whole series, and every routine is two steps by concern. It adds sound Klaviyo plumbing (entry filter, cart pause, WhatsApp only to non-clickers) and a holdout with correctly worked rupee value.
mistake: The WhatsApp and Email 5 say 'every other night' generically, so sunscreen-only recipients get night-use advice for a morning product. Also, no email ever pairs niacinamide with sunscreen as the morning step for the dark-spot path in the early emails.
to10: Fix the start-slow line per matched product, and say plainly in Email 1 or 2 that dark-spot readers need daily sunscreen alongside niacinamide.

strength: It ranks the 46 to 90 day 'slipping' group first with no discount, gives Monsoon Dark buyers their own track, and gates ex-subscribers on 93% on-time delivery plus pick-your-date. That is exactly how I read my own data.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark email asks customers to fill in a brew quiz instead of naming the closest roast up front. The ₹535 profit-per-subscriber figure and the specific calendar dates appear without explanation.
to10: Name the closest dark roast in the first Monsoon Dark email, and show proof of the delivery fix (the actual on-time rate) in the ex-subscriber message.

strength: The ex-subscriber track has a fix for each cancel reason and an email that proves the delivery fix with the live on-time rate. The Monsoon Dark email names the roasters' closest match.
mistake: It puts 91 to 180 days first and treats the cheap 46 to 90 day group as a side nudge rather than the top wave. Group A's 13,100 also contradicts its own claim that subscribers were removed from the other groups.
to10: Lead with a targeted, no-discount wave for the 9,000 at 46 to 90 days, and reconcile the group counts so no one is double-counted.

strength: It turns the diagnosis into a contribution baseline (13.6% a year ago, 7.8% now) and sizes every move in points of margin, with low/likely/high ranges, week-4 and week-8 kill lines and action thresholds. That is exactly the gross-profit ranking I asked for.
mistake: It is dense and number-heavy for a grade-8 read. It leans on an unsourced 'flows should be about half of email revenue' yardstick. The scorecard drops a line for flow revenue, even though rebuilding the flows is move 2.
to10: Add flow share of email revenue and the returns-cost line to the scorecard, and turn a few of the denser sizing paragraphs into plain sentences.

strength: It reads clearly and quickly. The checks table gives each item an owner and a deadline, there is a sensible week-by-week 90-day arc, and the scorecard includes flow share and the returns cost line. It also extends the returns fix to the other product lines.
mistake: The moves are ranked with vague 'high/medium' impact rather than sized gross profit, and contribution margin, the board's key number, is left as 'set baseline in week 1' when it could have been computed from the brief.
to10: Calculate the current contribution baseline and put a profit estimate on each move so the ranking rests on numbers rather than adjectives.

strength: It turns my top pair into a ₹999 three-step routine priced at the same ₹537 profit I'd work out myself, keeps ₹499 because that is where COD refusals drop from 29% to 17%, and adds a lip balm cart nudge plus a ₹49 COD fee test aimed at the ~800 refused small orders.
mistake: It is dense and number-heavy, with lakh ranges everywhere, so it takes a slow read. It also never prices a COD-only threshold, such as free shipping at ₹499 for prepaid and higher for COD, before jumping to a fee.
to10: Cut it down to a scannable page and work out the COD-versus-prepaid threshold split alongside the COD fee.

strength: A clean serum price ladder (₹599, ₹749, ₹999), clear per-bundle profit and break-even, and a sensible case for avoiding ₹699 because it puts the fee on Ishita's serum.
mistake: It recommends moving to ₹599 using an arbitrary assumption that only 6% of orders (~1,000) sit between ₹499 and ₹598, when the 27% band suggests about 2,300. It also leaves RTO out of the threshold maths and spends a bundle slot discounting the lip balm instead of using it as an add-on.
to10: Size the ₹499–598 slice from the actual band data, put COD refusal cost into the threshold decision, and use the lip balm as a cart add-on so the third bundle can be body care.

strength: It puts the in-app checkout bug first with the money (₹17–34 lakh gross profit a month), then gives five ranked tests whose detectable effects (9.9%, 6.3%, 5.5%) match the real traffic, each with a profit value and calendar dates.
mistake: Using add to cart as the main metric for the size and reviews tests and valuing them on an assumed 'half reaches orders' is a soft link to profit. There is also no per-browser diagnostic table to show where mobile leaks beyond the bug.
to10: Add a short device-by-browser funnel table and replace the ₹X EMI placeholder with a worked example, so the owner can see every leak and paste the copy straight away.

strength: A sharp diagnostic table by device and browser, and the check that the 4,130 in-app errors nearly match the 4,800 lost in-app carts, make the bug case airtight. Adding an A/A test and event tracking before testing is mature practice.
mistake: Test 5 bundles the hero image and the reviews move into one variant, so a win cannot be attributed to either change. Hypotheses also lack the minimum lift they are sized for, and tests carry no money value.
to10: Split test 5 into separate hero and reviews tests, and state each hypothesis with its detectable lift and gross-profit value.

strength: It works out RTO loss per order by pincode tier (₹70, ₹41, ₹27) and builds a different confirmation, nudge and cancel rule for each tier. Tier 3 gets the hardest treatment, with calls and a ₹40 UPI saving sized below its loss.
mistake: It says each discount 'sits below the loss it removes' without accounting for switchers who would never have refused, so the tier discounts could cost more than they save. The holdout only covers calls and cancels, not the discount.
to10: Add a no-discount holdout for the prepaid nudge, and give the after-hours bot a size-guide button so the 21% fit questions also get an instant answer at night.

strength: Clean templates with good flow mechanics: quiet hours, a confirm-then-chat-window nudge, and a holdout on the prepaid switch. Moving one agent to a 2 pm to midnight shift for the evening wave is a smart, cheap fix.
mistake: The 'pay by UPI now' nudge is filed as a Utility template. Meta is likely to recategorise it, and I said I didn't want marketing inside Utility. It also gives Tier 3 no stronger nudge and no money breakdown by tier, so the risk targeting stays weak.
to10: Make the prepaid nudge a Marketing template with an incentive sized per pincode tier, show the ₹ RTO cost by tier, and swap the size-chart homework in the cart template for an offer to tell the customer their size.

strength: Each ad set gets a clear verdict with rupee working, a budget table that adds to ₹5,60,000, and a creative brief in Rohan's and Ananya's words, so the team can start Monday.
mistake: It scales Catalog DPA and ramps ASC while using the Meta-count break-even as the main yardstick. DPA at frequency 5.2 is probably over-counted, and the ₹282/₹394 two-line approach leaves the call ambiguous.
to10: Commit to one Shopify-adjusted break-even per ad set instead of two lines, and do not scale an over-counted, high-frequency DPA.

strength: It sets a separate attribution-adjusted break-even for each ad set (86% for prospecting, 72% for retargeting and catalog), states the real account loss, and opens with concrete first moves: relaunch the creator video, cut Starter Kit and Gift Sets, narrow women to 25 to 34.
mistake: It puts ₹56,000 into a UGC test running at ₹581 per purchase against a ₹359 break-even, and it labels Retargeting a "cut" while still giving it ₹28,000, so the call counts don't match the table.
to10: Fund the UGC test at a capped, smaller amount and make the retargeting label match its budget, and cut the geo-holdout section down to one line the team can run.

strength: The day-30 verdict is tied to the 90-day break-even ($38.46) and read three ways (store tags, survey, blended lift against baseline), with a holdout as a fourth. The phased budget adds to exactly $30,000 and has a dollar release rule for days 21 to 30.
mistake: It is very dense, with tables everywhere and probably slightly over the word limit. It also assumes two new posts ("Clogs test", "Hour ten") from the existing creators that may not exist.
to10: Trim it to fit the word limit and plainly mark which creator posts already exist and which must be commissioned. The rest is already strong.

strength: It is a clean, Monday-ready plan with a Week 0 checklist, named owners, banned words restated, price handled inside the ad rather than with a discount, and budget phases (including the $1,000 reserve) that add to $30,000.
mistake: The day-30 pass bar leans mainly on TikTok-reported cost per first order. The incrementality check is a single row and the survey is only a secondary check. It also adds a separate Smart+ Scale campaign that muddies the read.
to10: Make the day-30 decision rest on the 90-day break-even with store, survey and holdout reads that must agree, and give more worked hook scripts in Maria's words.

strength: The first-three pick is tied to the data, with women 25 to 40 first, and it comes with a worked test budget (15 purchases each, about ₹63,000 in total) and stop rules that check out against the brief's numbers.
mistake: Some concepts are thin or familiar (the gift static, the four-specs Reel), and a few visuals hint at lightness (a one-hand lift into a cab) while the copy says quiet and light only appear as buyers' own lines.
to10: Make the last two or three concepts as fresh as the sound demo, and use Meera's and Karan's exact words in the primary text of more concepts.

strength: It gives each concept an explicit awareness level and a clear test, and a sound-led 5 am Reel, a solo-woman lift concept and a belt-skip concept are well argued.
mistake: It is less finished: there are no headlines, no size or safe-zone specs and no test budget in rupees, and the lift concept's primary text is generic and uses little of Meera's own language.
to10: Add headlines and a budget per concept, and put more real review and survey wording into the hooks and primary text, especially for the solo-woman concept.

strength: Three different angles (blind sip, 3 pm swap, game-day kids) each built on a real comment theme and the $26/$32 vs $44 data, with disclosure written into every brief and a costed hook-test plan with cut-off rules.
mistake: It runs well over the 1,300-word limit (roughly 1,800) because of added rights, contract terms and a bonus idea, and a few spoken lines are awkward, such as 'It's linked right there' while clinking cans.
to10: Cut it to 1,300 words by trimming the rights and delivery boilerplate, and make the alternate hooks change exactly one thing each.

strength: Clean, scannable scripts with sound angles and a natural, honest price answer ('It's my one soda of the day, so I want a good one'). Every ad closes on 'A new kind of soda.'
mistake: The testing guidance is thin with no budgets or kill rules, and disclosure is only a caption '#ad' plus platform toggles, with nothing on screen or spoken, which is weaker than it should be for paid creators. It also exceeds the word limit, though by less.
to10: Add per-hook spend and cut thresholds tied to the $26 and $32 benchmarks, put on-screen and spoken disclosure into every script, and stay under 1,300 words.

strength: Six truly different angles in Aditya's and Priya's own words. It brings back the paused ₹210 winner in fresh wording, leads with taste, and tackles the ₹90 price head-on. It adds a clean test design, with budget maths that checks out (5 cells × ₹1,200 × 14 days = ₹84,000).
mistake: It uses 27 characters as the limit for headlines and descriptions, which is stricter than needed. The 5-cell test with a control and the ₹84,000 spend is also an assumption the owner never gave.
to10: State the Meta limits as a single rule and note that the budget is adjustable, then offer a lighter-spend version of the test.

strength: A clear read of the past 90 days, with each of the four launch ads tied to one question (comeback, taste, label reader, price). It also supplies backup copy in case review quotes are not allowed.
mistake: Four of the six primary texts repeat "12 g protein / no added sugar", the sameness the owner dislikes. The 4 pm angle is weak and the gym angle is missing.
to10: Make each primary text open on a different hook without repeating the spec line, and add a budget split with concrete day-to-day rules.

strength: Puts the cash number (about 10 flat notes, total) in the subtitle, bullets, button line, specs and FAQ, handles the break-in, and shows return maths (3.3 per 100 orders, about 1.0 per 100 for early 'too tight') with a measurement plan and conversion fallback.
mistake: The first-week break-in note is missing from the bullets and the button line, so it sits lower down where some buyers won't see it. The 'Browse our other wallets' link is also a placeholder-style path.
to10: Move the 'snug for the first week, then it settles' note into a bullet or the button line, and drop the extra measurement section in favour of tighter page copy.

strength: Puts the break-in expectation in a bullet and states the trade-offs plainly ('We would rather tell you now than have you send it back'), with a clear 'what fits in real life' scenario list.
mistake: Invents a hidden pocket that takes one extra note beyond the 10, which risks overstating cash capacity, the very thing driving 44% of returns. It also says the slots are tight 'so cards stay put' and that the wallet sits flat in a back pocket, neither of which is in the data.
to10: Stick to the given 'about 10 notes' with no invented extra capacity, and explain what the break-in and cash expectations are worth in returns.

strength: It uses all three data signals: it leads with the best-converting niacinamide for the 55% with tone, dullness or no answer, it gives the sunscreen leak (2.2% order rate, white cast and stickiness questions) its own email with the 'dusky skin' review, and it builds a slow-start plan for the 61% who are new to actives. It also adds a holdout test and a gross-profit estimate.
mistake: It probably runs slightly over the 1,800-word limit, and it spends space on test and projection sections the owner didn't ask for. Email 5's 'one active at night' wording is also a little loose.
to10: Trim to the word limit, and give the dark-spot routine (sunscreen plus niacinamide) its own focused email instead of folding it into the product match and Email 5.

strength: Email 2 has three versions split on the quiz answer, and the sunscreen FAQ email answers white cast, stickiness and makeup with the review quote.
mistake: Email 5 sends everyone the same routine of face wash, sunscreen and serum, ₹1,297 in total. That contradicts its own 'one product at a time' advice and its advice to dry or sensitive readers not to start with an acid.
to10: Personalise Email 5 by quiz answer, replace the cosmetic claims like 'helps clear out oil' with calmer wording, and add a holdout and a worth estimate.

strength: It starts with the 46 to 90 day group using a no-discount reminder, gives Monsoon Dark buyers their own track, and gates ex-subscribers behind a delivery fix, with a dated week-one plan and a 10% holdout per group.
mistake: The worth table ignores WhatsApp-only reach and uses an unexplained ₹535 profit per returner for G6. The Monsoon Dark draft promises a match but never names it, and there is no explicit break-even lift per group.
to10: Name the actual closest dark roast and farm in the Monsoon Dark draft, show the break-even lift per offer, and trim to the 1,500-word limit.

strength: It states plainly that lapsed buyers left because something broke, not over price. It gates ex-subscribers on delivery, and adds a day-28 running-low nudge plus offer tests (10% vs free shipping) judged on gross profit.
mistake: It launches with the 91 to 180 day group and treats the 46 to 90 day group only as an always-on nudge, not a first wave. The worth model also puts 2 orders per returner in a 12-month ₹8.5 lakh figure, subtracts discount cost twice, and uses holdout sizes that don't match contactable counts.
to10: Make the 46 to 90 day group wave one with a no-discount reminder, use a conservative reachable base with a break-even lift, and fill the match placeholders with a real named roast.

strength: It puts numbers on everything: a contribution baseline (7.8% against 13.6%), a sized gain for each move in margin points, and a scorecard with week-4 and week-8 lines and action thresholds. Meta's 68% cost rise and the linen returns fault sit at the centre.
mistake: The baseline and per-move gains rest on stacked assumptions (flat order values, "half new", a flow-share yardstick). Some gains are false precision, and the page is dense and close to the word limit.
to10: The same quantified plan with fewer stacked assumptions, a lighter page, and a plain first-week task list per owner.

strength: It is clear and well reasoned. It shows each Meta customer losing $27 over 18 months, pairs each open question with an owner and a due week, and gives a clean stop list and a phased 90 days.
mistake: Moves are ranked only as High, Medium or Low, with no gross profit figure per move. The scorecard has no contribution baseline ("set baseline in week 1"), so the board's key metric is left unquantified.
to10: Compute the contribution baseline and put a dollar or margin-point gain next to each ranked move, with action thresholds on the scorecard.

strength: A clear ₹599 / ₹699 comparison with break-even step-up counts for each bundle, plus a sensible bundle ladder on the serum page.
mistake: The ₹599 recommendation rests on a guessed 6% of orders sitting in the ₹499–598 band, which is too low given the 27% in ₹500–699. COD refusals are barely used in the threshold decision and no COD fee or prepaid idea is considered, so the +₹28k gain is weak.
to10: Size the affected order band from the given spread, build COD/RTO cost into the threshold choice, and make the face wash + serum routine bundle the lead with a plain two-item version.

strength: It uses COD refusal rates and the ₹130 RTO cost to shape the whole threshold answer: keep ₹499, add a lip balm cart offer for orders under ₹499, and try a ₹49 COD fee. It also explains why Glow Routine adds a lip balm rather than cutting the pair's price.
mistake: The threshold advice is somewhat hedged: it keeps ₹499 but wants a ₹699 test with a wide −₹0.72 to +₹2.35 lakh range. The answer is also dense with numbers and runs near the word limit.
to10: Commit to one threshold with a point estimate, trim the density, and show the working behind the ₹60/₹91 lift per lip-balm add.

strength: It calls the in-app checkout bug first, sizes it correctly (~1,860 checkouts, ~560 orders, ~₹34 lakh margin), and covers all five chat topics, including a separate firmness test with a 100-night return check.
mistake: Firmness rating and EMI amount are left as bracketed blanks. Orders per session is the main metric for the size-picker test, which stretches it to 4 weeks, and the bug fix is not tied explicitly to keeping test results clean.
to10: Fill the placeholders, use add-to-cart as the main metric where it fits the size test, and state plainly that the fix must land before any test starts so in-app traffic does not pollute results.

strength: It opens with the in-app bug and its money range, says tests start only after the fix, and sizes every test to the real traffic. It also notes that add-to-cart is the wrong metric for the delivery and EMI tests and uses gross profit as the guardrail.
mistake: It has no standalone firmness test (only reviews tabs) and gives less customer-facing copy in the brand voice. The dense rules and fixed calendar dates read as heavy.
to10: Add ready-to-paste trial and delivery lines in the brand voice and tighten the rules section.

strength: The flow is tiered by pincode risk. Tier 3 gets the call and cancel rule, and each prepaid discount (₹20 for Tier 2, ₹40 for Tier 3) is sized against that tier's expected RTO loss. Holdouts and a net-saving metric back it up.
mistake: The calling workload falls on the same 4 chat agents with no staffing change, and the after-hours cover is only a bot menu, so size and exchange questions at night just wait until morning.
to10: Add a staffing or shift change for the evening wave and tighten the length, so the plan stands on its own with no other changes.

strength: It sends the prepaid nudge as a free-form chat message right after Confirm, inside the open 24-hour window, and it moves one agent to a 2 pm to midnight shift to cover the evening wave.
mistake: Prepaid handling is the same for every pincode group, with no incentive and no per-tier loss working. Template 3, "skip cash at the door", is promotional but is submitted as Utility, so it risks recategorisation.
to10: Work out expected RTO loss per order by pincode group, scale the prepaid push and the confirmation firmness to each tier, and file the prepaid nudge under Marketing.

strength: It judges every ad set on order value after COD refusals, with its own break-even, then forecasts the result honestly: the plan cuts the loss from about −₹1.2 lakh to about −₹33,000 on the store's count, and it says plainly that nothing has earned a raise yet.
mistake: The 86% 'real purchases' figure for prospecting is a loosely argued midpoint, and labelling retargeting 'Cut' when it is only halved muddles the verdicts.
to10: Justify the attribution haircut with the Shopify data instead of a midpoint, and use plainer labels and a simpler table so a non-expert can act on it in two minutes.

strength: Very clear: the two-line idea (a safe line and a break-even line), a separate budget table that adds to ₹5.6 lakh, a creative brief in Rohan's and Ananya's words, and a sharp lesson that pausing the creator video cost about ₹65,000.
mistake: It scales ASC and catalog against Meta-count break-even, which breaks its own 'scale only under the safe line' rule. ASC's gate of ₹320 sits above its own ₹282 safe line, so it can buy money-losing orders.
to10: Make the scaling gates match its own safe lines, and don't scale catalog at frequency 5.2 without a holdout check.

strength: Gets the money right ($27.10 first order, about $38.50 over 90 days, $38 target), runs the nurse and server Spark Ads from day 1, and phases a budget that adds to $30,000 with dollar kill and scale rules.
mistake: The family and mission concepts are thin: Concept 5's hook is just 'Same as Concept 1', and few hooks use Maria's or Tasha's exact words.
to10: Write every hook in the customers' own phrases and add a geo holdout so the day-30 call doesn't rest only on a before-and-after comparison.

strength: A Monday-ready plan: no spend until the test order passes, a learning bar worked out in dollars, 12 hooks written in Maria's and Tasha's own words, and a day-30 verdict that needs two of three independent reads plus a state holdout.
mistake: The day-21 release rule counts TikTok-reported cost as one of its three reads, so platform numbers can help unlock the scale budget.
to10: Replace the TikTok-reported read in the release rule with the holdout or blended lift, and say how many new on-feet creators to brief and when.

strength: Primary text is short, calm and in our voice. The data read is sharp: women are 26% of purchases on 18% of spend, and it adds a worked illustration of what lowering men's cost per purchase is worth.
mistake: Its rule of 'about ₹4,500 per concept' (three times blended cost) is too little spend to judge whether to scale. It is really a stop-loss rule passed off as a test budget.
to10: Add headlines and a proper test budget per concept, and put the cheaper women's audience first, as the data supports.

strength: Ready to hand to a team. It gives headlines with character counts, Reels safe zones, scene timings, a worked test budget per concept (15 purchases of spend, ₹63,000 total), and it handles both the scuff and front-pocket objections.
mistake: Primary text runs longer and more spec-heavy than our short-line voice. Concepts 2 and 8 are statics that drift back toward the product shots we already have.
to10: Cut the primary text to short calm lines, and turn one of the two statics into a fresher format.

strength: It ties every script to my own cost-per-purchase and comment data, and it points out that label reads got the most spend ($24,000) despite costing $44 a purchase. It then adds a test plan with real numbers ($800 an ad, cut below a 19% view rate) plus rights and deliverables.
mistake: Putting the spoken 'Olipop paid me' line in the middle of the blind taste test interrupts the payoff moment. It also runs past the 1,300-word limit.
to10: Move the spoken disclosure out of the blind sip, sharpen the price answer beyond '12 afternoons for me', and trim to the word limit.

strength: The voice is playful and on brand ('Still fizzy. Still sweet. Still my treat.'), and the creator briefs are smart, such as how to recover if the friend guesses right in the blind test.
mistake: The test plan is thin, with no budget or cut rules. The 3 pm hook ('You know what that means') is vaguer than my customers' own words, and price is handled in only one script.
to10: Add a numbered test budget with kill and scale rules, and open Script 2 with 'My 3 pm soda' taken straight from the comments.

strength: It brings back the paused ₹210 winner in fresh words, tests taste and price head-on, and gives six truly different angles in Aditya's and Priya's own words, each with a character count.
mistake: Ad B pairs the taste text with a protein headline, so a win won't show cleanly whether taste or protein did the work.
to10: Pair the taste text with a taste-led headline built from 'Doesn't taste like a protein bar', so test B isolates taste cleanly.

strength: It reads the data well: the fatigued winner, the never-run taste phrase and the price objection. It also adds a sensible backup in case legal blocks the review quotes.
mistake: Almost every primary text ends on '12 g protein. No added sugar.' That makes the set feel like six versions of one ad, and two of the four launch slots go to the same transparency angle.
to10: Cut the repeated spec line from each text, give the 4 pm snack its own witty angle in Priya's words, and set a real budget and a control cell for the test.

strength: It names the cash limit and the first-week tightness everywhere a buyer looks, including a bullet above the fold, and it has a frank 'What to know before you buy' paragraph that fits our honest voice.
mistake: It invents an extra note in the hidden pocket ('takes one more flat note'), which risks overstating cash capacity, the very cause of 44% of returns, even though it flags this as an assumption.
to10: Treat about 10 flat notes as the total, put the break-in note under the add-to-cart button, and add a simple way to measure whether returns fall.

strength: It states cash conservatively as about 10 notes in total, hidden pocket included. It uses Tom's 'brick in your back pocket' phrase and adds inch conversions for US buyers. It ends with a measurement plan and correct return maths (about 3.3 and 1.0 per 100 orders) with a conversion guardrail.
mistake: The break-in warning is missing from the bullets and the line under the button, and the '10 to 11 mm' figure for 6 or 7 cards is an interpolation the data doesn't give.
to10: Move 'snug for the first week, then it settles' into a bullet or under the button, and stick to the stated thickness figures.

strength: Email 4 answers the white cast, stickiness and makeup questions with the dusky-skin review, and Email 2 splits by quiz answer so each person gets one product in our calm voice.
mistake: Email 5 sends every buyer a salicylic wash twice a day plus niacinamide plus sunscreen. That breaks the one-product, no-acid advice it just gave dry and sensitive skin, and calls four slots '3 steps'.
to10: Make Email 5 match each quiz answer, as Email 2 does, and add a holdout and a money estimate so I can tell whether the series pays.

strength: It matches people from the quiz in Email 1 and carries that match through every email. Email 5 gives a separate short routine for each concern, with correct prices, and the projections are all right: ₹48 vs ₹9 per click, about ₹32,900 per extra point.
mistake: The plain-text emails skip a greeting, and prices like ₹628.20 with paise read awkwardly in customer copy.
to10: Round the code prices, add a short greeting, and flag the texture and makeup claims to check against the product page.

strength: The Monsoon Dark email names the discontinued blend and the roasters' closest match, and the subscriber track is held behind a 93% on-time gate that leads with pick-your-date.
mistake: The 9,000 slipping customers at 46 to 90 days, who are the cheapest to win back, are only an aside (a day-28 nudge) and are not first in the ranked plan, while the ₹8.5 lakh rests on a generous two-orders-per-returner assumption.
to10: Put the 46 to 90 day group first with its count and reach, remove ex-subscribers from the other groups as promised, and show the break-even lift for each group.

strength: It ranks the slipping 46 to 90 day buyers first with no discount, removes overlap between groups, and builds a careful profit range (₹557, ₹442 and ₹385 per order, ₹535 blended for ex-subscribers) after the holdout.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark draft sends people to a quiz instead of naming the closest coffee still on sale, which weakens the one-clear-fix track.
to10: Name the roasters' match in the Monsoon Dark email, and count WhatsApp-only reach in the value table instead of email reach alone.

strength: A clean, readable diagnosis that pins the cost rise on Meta and linen, with correct working: $71 contribution, $33 loss per first order, $94 18-month value, linen adding 1.8 points of returns.
mistake: The impact column is mostly High/Medium/Low rather than sized in profit, and the scorecard leaves key targets vague ('pre-January level', 'set baseline in week 1'), so the moves are not truly ranked by gross profit.
to10: Size each move in contribution dollars or points with the working, and give every scorecard line a hard number and a trigger.

strength: Turns the plan into a contribution-margin model: today's baseline of about 7.8% against 13.6% a year ago, each move sized low/likely/high in points, week-4 and week-8 go/stop lines, and action thresholds on every scorecard row.
mistake: Several sizings rest on stacked assumptions (Meta holding the same customers at $100, 'half new' revenue, an unsourced 'about half' flow benchmark), and the density makes it harder to read than it needs to be.
to10: Keep the model, but simplify the wording for a non-expert and flag more plainly which gains depend on the week-1 tracking and linen checks.

strength: It builds the plan around the real money leak: a ₹199 lip balm cart add-on lifts small carts over ₹499, it sizes the COD refusal cost under ₹499 (₹1.04 lakh a month), and it proposes a ₹49 COD fee test, while the bundles mirror the pairs people already buy.
mistake: The threshold table does not show how COD refusals change in each scenario, and the dense lakh figures and break-even per-order values (₹262 and others) come without enough working for a non-expert to follow.
to10: Show the ₹599 and ₹699 maths line by line with refusal cost included, and consider free shipping at a lower bar for prepaid orders only.

strength: It explains in plain words, with a clear outcome table, why ₹599 beats ₹699 (the serum-only reorder stays free), and the pricing ladder on the serum page is easy to follow.
mistake: It assumes only 6% of orders fall between ₹499 and ₹598 when an even spread of the 27% band gives about 13%, which understates the risk of raising the threshold, and it leaves COD refusals out of the threshold decision.
to10: Recalculate the ₹599 slice from the order-value spread, bring COD refusal cost into the threshold choice, and use the lip balm as a cart add-on with a body or hair routine as the second bundle instead of a discounted serum and lip balm set.

strength: The funnel table is correct and sized by browser, and it spots that about 4,130 in-app pop-up errors almost match the 4,800 in-app carts that never reach checkout, so the bug fix is money I can bank (₹34 lakh a month).
mistake: Every test, including the 30-plus size picker, is read on orders per session, so the plan stretches to 11 weeks, and the firmness rating and EMI amounts are left as blanks.
to10: Use add to cart where it reads faster on mobile, shorten the schedule, and fill in real firmness and EMI wording so it can go live at once.

strength: The rigour is honest. It says no test starts until the in-app fix is live, explains why add to cart would mislead on the delivery and EMI tests, warns that no-cost EMI eats margin, and sets no-peeking, split-check and ship rules with real dates.
mistake: Firmness, the second biggest chat topic, gets no test of its own and is only folded into a review filter, and the sample delivery date of '1 Dec' clashes with the couple's move-in on the 10th.
to10: Add a plain-words firmness test and lighten the dense sections so a non-expert can scan them faster.

strength: A complete, pincode-aware confirmation flow with shipped and out-for-delivery messages, an after-hours bot, and a smart idea to move one agent to a 2 pm to midnight shift for the 31% evening wave.
mistake: The prepaid nudge carries no incentive and is filed as Utility, so it gives Tier 3, where half the RTO money sits, no stronger push than a metro buyer gets; it also assumes a 7-day exchange window that may not be ours.
to10: Size a prepaid incentive per pincode tier against the RTO loss it removes, submit it as Marketing, and add a net-saving metric to the scorecard.

strength: Works out the RTO loss per COD order by tier (₹70 / ₹41 / ₹27) and sizes each prepaid discount below that loss, with calls and a firm 48-hour cancel only for Tier 3, plus holdouts to prove the saving.
mistake: The cart template says 'Cash on delivery is on' for every cart, which is wrong where COD isn't offered on that pincode, and it misses staffing the evening shift.
to10: Add a prepaid-only cart variant for non-COD pincodes and shift one agent into the 8 pm to midnight window alongside the night bot.

strength: It makes the owner's three key moves with rupee reasons: relaunch the paused creator video first, narrow Women Body Razor to 25 to 34, and cut the COD-heavy Starter Kit. The budget adds to ₹5,60,000 and gives a clear ASC scaling ladder.
mistake: The two-line safe/break-even framework leaves ad sets in an ambiguous middle zone. It also scales Catalog DPA at frequency 5.2 and implies the Starter Kit buyers are the ones who refuse, which blames the COD customers.
to10: Use one Shopify-adjusted break-even per ad set, add a way to test whether retargeting and DPA really add sales, and keep to the word limit.

strength: Each ad set gets one break-even built from its own order value, COD share and RTO rate, adjusted for Shopify attribution. The release rules for the reserve are exact, and the geo holdout for retargeting is a fresh, rigorous idea.
mistake: It makes zero scale calls and holds a ₹1,49,100 reserve back, which is cautious when the warehouse can ship 3x. It also cuts retargeting, which is profitable on Meta's own count, on a harsh haircut.
to10: Commit more of the budget to the relaunched creator video in ASC and the women 25 to 34 split on day one, and trim the density to stay inside the word limit.

strength: A complete Monday-ready plan: tracking set-up, nurse and server Spark Ads from day 1, a budget that adds to $30,000, kill and scale rules in dollars, and a day-30 scorecard tied to the $38 target and an own-store new-customer check.
mistake: The hooks are thin and not in Maria's and Tasha's own words (Concept 5 just says 'Same as Concept 1'), and the day-30 table mixes Pass/Hold/Fail thresholds without saying which source of orders decides.
to10: Write every hook in the customers' real phrases, state one clear source of truth for the day-30 verdict, and add a holdout or a stronger incrementality check.

strength: Ready-to-shoot creative that opens on the foot problem in the customers' own words ('My feet don't ache by hour ten', 'Pricey, but I'm never going back') and closes with 'One purchased = one donated' as a fact, supported by shown working for every threshold ($27.10, $38.46, $57, the learning bar).
mistake: The day-30 release rule is somewhat convoluted, with a $50 store-tag threshold and three reads. Even a pass only 'holds' spend at about $1,625 a day, so it is cautious about scaling.
to10: Simplify the day-20 and day-30 decision into one clear primary read with the others as checks, and say what to do when the licensed Spark posts expire in March.

strength: Eight distinct concepts with hooks lifted from customer language. Each has a clear awareness level and test, and the data work is right (26% of purchases on 18% of spend, ₹292 a trip, ₹1,515 blended cost).
mistake: Some copy drifts from the brand voice and the approved claims. "Zero belt time" and "Quiet wheels are the top theme in our 1,150 reviews" read as stats, not understated copy. The scuff objection is only a brief assumption and does not shape the visuals.
to10: Add headlines and exact shot or format specs, keep every line strictly within approved claims and the brand voice, and show how the scuff problem changes each visual.

strength: It handles the data signals and brand risks head-on. The first three put women 25 to 40 first, then belt-skip, then quiet wheels. It names the scuff and front-pocket problems and sets claim rules (review lines only, no scratch implication). Each concept comes with headline, sizes and a test budget.
mistake: It ignores the 41-plus audience, and some concepts (the specs reel, the gift static) are plainer. The one-hand cab lift in concept 1 hints at lightness beyond the specs.
to10: Give each concept its own one-line test variable and success threshold instead of leaving it in a table, and add a concept or note for the underperforming 41-plus group.

strength: Three distinct angles (blind test, 3 pm swap, family cooler), each with timed shot list, two alternate hooks and a creator brief, with price answered in the 3 pm script.
mistake: Script 3 and the pack lines use hooks like 'my kids think this is regular soda' as a flat claim, and there is no on-screen 'Ad' from the first frame. Disclosure sits only in the caption and toggles, and the test plan is thin with no budget or kill rules.
to10: Add budget and kill rules for the hook test, visible disclosure inside each video, and a stronger answer to the $3 objection in all three scripts.

strength: It ties each script to the cost-per-purchase data and comment shares, answers price on camera, writes disclosure into each script, and adds a numbered test plan with budget and cut rules plus a bolder reply-video idea.
mistake: Some lines are crowded and the sub-claims overload scripts (for example the three-claim line in script 2), and the fixed $800 per ad budget is tight for the stated purchase counts. It also runs past the 1,300-word limit and is dense.
to10: Trim the density and word count, and make the price answer more vivid, for example a coffee-shop comparison.

strength: It brings back the paused front-of-pack winner and tests taste in a clean first four, with character counts shown and every line inside the limits.
mistake: The six primary texts are not six distinct angles. P1 and P5 both say transparency, P2 and P3 both lean on review quotes, and protein and the 4 pm snack get no real angle. The price line just states ₹90 and never answers the objection.
to10: Give each of the six texts a truly different angle, with Priya's samosa and 4 pm words and a price line that answers the daily-habit objection, and add budget and stop rules for the launch.

strength: The six angles are genuinely different and use Aditya's and Priya's own words (samosa, 4 pm, chalky). The launch plan makes the four ads lead with transparency, taste and price. Its budget, control cell and kill and fatigue rules are built from the brief's numbers.
mistake: Leading P4 with the customer's quote "₹90 a bar is a lot for every day" is a bold brand risk, and it never frames ₹90 against a daily alternative such as a samosa.
to10: Frame the ₹90 against a real daily alternative and offer a softer price line as a fallback in case the quote-first version feels too exposed.

strength: Puts the 10-note cash figure in the subtitle, bullets, spec, FAQ and under-button line, sets the first-week snugness expectation, and includes a measurement plan with correct return math (3.3 and about 1.0 per 100 orders).
mistake: Adds a measurement section and a 'not the right wallet for you' line that go beyond the brief; the 'sweet spot 10 to 11 mm' figure for 6 or 7 cards is slightly extrapolated.
to10: Make the first-week break-in note visible in the above-the-fold bullets or under the button, and drop the extrapolated thickness figure.

strength: Frank 'what to know before you buy' paragraph and a 'what fits' ladder (light day, full day, most it takes) that state the cash limit plainly, plus a break-in note in a bullet.
mistake: Invents that the hidden pocket holds one extra flat note beyond the 10, which risks overstating cash capacity, the very thing driving returns, and it contradicts the 'about 10' in the brief.
to10: Remove the invented extra-note claim and state that the hidden pocket is part of the roughly 10-note total.

strength: It reads the data and acts on it: each person gets one product matched to their quiz answer, the sunscreen doubts get their own email using the 'no white cast' review, and the exit rule, cart pause and code deadline are all worked out in detail.
mistake: It is dense and probably runs past the 1,800-word cap, with a long data preamble and a test section the owner didn't ask for. The sunscreen email also leans on application tips that aren't confirmed against the product.
to10: Cut the extra material to fit the word limit, and add a quiz-matched dark-spot routine that pairs sunscreen with niacinamide inside Email 1 or 2, so the series leads harder with the 44% segment.

strength: Email 2 has three quiz-matched versions with their own subject lines and a 'start slowly' line, which answers 'I don't know which serum is for me' well.
mistake: Email 5 tells everyone to use the acid face wash morning and night plus the serum and sunscreen. That is a full routine for beginners and contradicts the one-product, go-slow message in the other emails.
to10: Make the final routine two steps matched to the quiz answer, remove invented claims such as 'more questions than anything else we sell' and the 'brightening' example, and make Email 1 do more than a generic welcome.

strength: It puts the 46 to 90 day group first with no code, gives Monsoon Dark its own track and gates ex-subscribers on a delivery fix. Group counts are netted so nothing overlaps, and the profit table is worked from ₹557 and ₹442 per order.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark email only sends people to a quiz and never names the closest match. It also hard-codes dates and a 'stopped in March' claim, and the whole piece is dense and probably over the 1,500-word limit.
to10: Name the closest match in the Monsoon Dark email, trim the length with plainer words, and state the break-even lift for each group.

strength: It says plainly that people left because something broke, not over price. It names the match in the Monsoon Dark draft, gates ex-subscribers on on-time delivery, and ties each cancel reason to a fix.
mistake: It starts with the 91 to 180 day group and treats the 9,000 at-risk customers at 46 to 90 days as a later day-28 nudge. That misses the cheapest win-back and leaves the first wave less sharp.
to10: Make the 46 to 90 day group wave one with a light reminder, then fill the draft placeholders with real examples. Also work out the break-even lift for each group.

strength: A clean, plain-language split of proved facts from checks, with working that traces to my data: Meta would have blended to about $79, a loss of $33 per first order, and $94 as the 18-month breakeven. Every check and move has an owner.
mistake: Moves are ranked by High/Medium/Low rather than a single gross-profit number, and the '$100k cut adds $23k to $41k' line is loosely supported. I can't tell how much each move is worth to the board's contribution goal.
to10: Size each move in contribution points or dollars with the working shown, add action thresholds to the scorecard, and give a firm contribution target instead of 'set a baseline in week 1'.

strength: It rebuilds a contribution baseline (7.8% now against 13.6% a year ago) and sizes every move in contribution points with low, likely and high cases. That is the exact lens the board asked for.
mistake: It is dense and a little jargon-heavy (gain ranges, week 4/8 lines, stacked assumptions). The 'practitioner yardstick' on flows and the dated calendar are not grounded in my data.
to10: Keep the quantified ranking but write it in plainer words with fewer stacked assumptions, and drop the ungrounded benchmark.

strength: It ties the threshold decision to COD refusals, using the 29% vs 17% RTO split, the ₹130 and ₹70 costs, a lip-balm cart add-on for sub-₹499 carts and a ₹49 COD-fee test, and it covers three product categories with break-even for each bundle.
mistake: It is dense and likely over the word limit, with many lakh-level projections built on stacked assumptions. It also keeps ₹499 without fully working out the 27% band between ₹500 and 699, leaving that to a test.
to10: Tighten it to plain, grade 6 to 7 prose under 1,300 words, and show a worked per-order gross-profit comparison for the ₹500 to 699 band at ₹499 against ₹699, split by COD and prepaid.

strength: It is clear and easy to act on: a price ladder on the serum page, break-even per bundle, the point that ₹599 keeps Ishita's serum free, and a tidy test plan with stop rules.
mistake: It guesses that only about 6% of orders sit at ₹499 to 598 (the data suggests more) and builds the ₹599 maths on that. It barely uses the COD/RTO data in the threshold decision, and the serum + lip balm bundle is not really a routine.
to10: Estimate the affected order share from the order-value spread and put COD refusals (₹130) into the threshold maths by order band. Replace the serum + lip balm bundle with a body or hair routine, and use the lip balm as a cart add-on.

strength: It opens with the in-app checkout bug, sized correctly (1,860 more checkouts, about 558 orders, ₹34 lakh a month) and fixed before any test. Sample sizes are honest and right: 9.9% on orders per session, 6.3% on mobile add to cart, each with a rupee value.
mistake: Test 5 (hero image) rests on thin evidence and takes a slot that a firmness test could have used. The text is also dense, with jargon like "server-side split" and "named segment", and it runs over 1,500 words.
to10: Plainer language, a firmness-in-plain-words test in place of the hero image, and a trimmed word count.

strength: The funnel table by device and browser makes the in-app bug obvious. It matches the 4,300 pop-up errors to the 4,800 in-app carts that never reach checkout. It also adds a firmness test that speaks to "too soft for us", and an A/A check.
mistake: Most tests use orders per session over four weeks with about 10 to 12% detectable lifts, and the schedule stretches to 11 weeks. Test 5 bundles hero image and reviews, so a result cannot be traced to either. There are no per-test money values.
to10: Cheaper add-to-cart reads where they fit, so the plan finishes sooner. Each test needs a rupee value, and the hero image and reviews should be tested separately. The firmness and EMI blanks should be filled with example copy.

strength: Complete, paste-ready templates with correct categories for most, plus clear event-based timing, an after-hours menu and a shift change for the 31% evening wave.
mistake: The prepaid nudge is the same for every pincode group, and the pay-online template is filed as Utility although it pushes a payment choice. Tier 3, which causes about half the RTO cost, gets only a firmer hold step.
to10: Size the prepaid nudge and the confirm window by pincode group, with a stronger Tier 3 offer, and file the payment push as Marketing.

strength: The flow is tiered by pincode risk. It works out expected RTO loss per COD order (₹70 / ₹41 / ₹27), sizes each prepaid discount below that loss, limits calls to Tier 3, and measures the result against holdouts and a net-saving metric.
mistake: The ₹20 and ₹40 discounts and the ₹99 advance projections are assumed, not drawn from the data, and the table format is a bit dense. The tool does not describe moving agent hours to cover the evening chats.
to10: Add a staffing change for the after-hours load and show the working behind the discount sizes and the ₹99 advance projection.

strength: Every ad set is judged on its own order value, COD share and refusal rate after the Shopify attribution haircut. That gives a store-count loss of −₹1,21,700 and a budget that sums exactly to ₹5,60,000, with ₹1,49,100 held back and released only by rule.
mistake: Retargeting is labelled 'Cut' even though the action is a halving, and prospecting assumes 86% of Meta's purchases are real, which is kinder than the 72% Shopify actually shows.
to10: Fix the retargeting label, show the forecast at a flat 72% as well as at 86%, and give the Starter Kit a prepaid-only route back instead of only cutting it.

strength: The two lines per ad set are easy for a team to follow, the numbers check out (ASC +₹30,400, Starter Kit break-even ₹271, Women 25 to 34 at ₹414), and the persona-led creative brief is ready to brief.
mistake: Decisions sit on Meta's count. Catalog is scaled, retargeting is held at ₹40,000 even though it loses money on Shopify numbers, and the ASC gate is ₹320, above its own ₹282 safe line.
to10: Make the safe line the trigger for scaling and holding, so no budget moves on Meta's inflated count, and add a prepaid or COD-confirmation fix for the Starter Kit.

strength: Gets the money right ($27.10 first order, about $38.50 over 90 days, a $38 target). It builds on the nurse and server Spark Ads, keeps the mission line as a closer, and has a phased budget that adds to exactly $30,000 with a reserve rule.
mistake: Some scorecard measures don't line up. It says to judge on days 15 to 30, yet the order target is 790 orders over all 30 days at $38, which ignores the learning-period cost. It also assumes the March licences cover the month instead of planning around them.
to10: Write every hook as a finished on-screen line in Maria's and Tasha's words, add a geo holdout, and make the day-30 targets match the days-15-to-30 window.

strength: Twelve ready-to-shoot hooks use the customers' own lines, including 'My feet don't ache by hour ten' and 'Pricey, but I'm never going back' to meet the price objection head-on. It also judges day 30 on three reads plus a state holdout, which gives a solid answer on whether TikTok brings new customers rather than claiming Meta's.
mistake: It plans only three new on-feet creators across the month and leans on staff phone videos, which is a thin pipeline for the style the data shows works. The 25-and-up age floor rests on weak reasoning.
to10: Brief 6 to 10 new on-feet worker creators from week 1 so owned winners are ready before the March licences end.

strength: Primary text is short and calm in our voice, hooks come straight from review and persona lines, and the first three (belt-skip, lift-it-yourself, 5 am quiet wheels) are tied to the right numbers.
mistake: The test budget of three times blended cost, about ₹4,500 per concept, is roughly three purchases, too thin to scale or cut on. The gift copy also states 'rolls quiet' as a brand claim rather than a buyer quote.
to10: Give each concept a realistic read budget and a headline, keep 'quiet' as quoted buyer words only, and add the shot-level detail an editor needs.

strength: Production-ready. It has scene timings, safe zones, headlines with character counts, quiet and light kept as buyers' own words, the front-pocket and scuff objections handled, and a costed read plan (15 purchases per concept, ₹63,000 total) that checks out.
mistake: The primary texts run as dense paragraphs rather than the short grade-7 lines our voice asks for, and the gift concept is a flat static that drifts back toward today's look.
to10: Break the primary text into short lines and give the gift concept a real moment instead of a doorway static.

strength: It is built on my own data: it leads with taste and the $26 blind test, keeps the label read until after the sip, and answers the $3-a-can objection in all three scripts. It then adds a test plan whose numbers check out ($800 × 9 = $7,200, a tenth of the $72,000 spent) along with deliverables, rights and timelines.
mistake: Some spoken lines are clunky and off-voice: 'Olipop paid me for this one' sits in the middle of the taste test, and '12 afternoons for me' is a weak answer on price. Script 2 also crams three claims into 7 seconds.
to10: Make the spoken lines warmer and more playful, and give the price a reason it's worth $3 (a treat, my one soda) instead of just doing the arithmetic.

strength: The scripts sound on-brand and are easy to say aloud ('Still fizzy. Still sweet. Still my treat.'), the price objection is handled well ('my one soda of the day, so I want a good one'), and the blind-test brief includes a smart pivot if the friend guesses right.
mistake: Price only comes up in one script. Script 3's alternate hook 'Real soda or not?' implies Olipop isn't real soda. The test plan has no budget, thresholds or cut rules, and there are no deliverables or usage rights.
to10: Add a numbered test plan with budget and cut rules, a deliverables-and-rights block, and a price answer in every script.

strength: It spots the paused ₹210 winner and the never-used taste reviews, and every line has a correct, tight character count.
mistake: Two of the four launch ads (A and C) are both transparency, and B pairs a taste text with a protein headline, so the test splits two ways and misses the full range of angles.
to10: Six truly separate angles, including a taste headline, with each launch ad isolating one variable against a live control.

strength: Six genuinely different angles in Aditya's and Priya's own words, launched as a clean A/B test with a control, one image, the budget maths (₹16,800 a cell, about 58 purchases at ₹290) and cut rules.
mistake: No headline leads with taste, and 'Looking for the hidden sugar in our protein bar?' brushes against the brief's rule about not scaring people.
to10: Add a taste headline close to 'Doesn't taste like a protein bar' and reword P3 so it doesn't hint at other brands hiding sugar.

strength: Puts both return drivers above the fold: 'about 10 notes laid flat' in the subtitle and a bullet, and 'slots start snug and ease in over about a week' in a bullet, backed by a frank 'What to know before you buy' section.
mistake: It assumes the hidden pocket takes one more note beyond the 10. That could overstate cash capacity on the very issue the page is meant to fix, although the assumption is flagged.
to10: Treat 10 notes as the total, use Tom's 'brick in my back pocket' language, and put the break-in note in the line under the button.

strength: Cash is stated conservatively as about 10 notes in total, hidden pocket included. It adds inches for US buyers, uses Tom's 'brick in your back pocket' line, and gives a measurement plan with the correct arithmetic: 3.3 cash returns and 1.0 early tight-slot returns per 100 orders, plus a conversion guardrail.
mistake: The break-in expectation is missing from the bullets and the line under the button. Also, '10 to 11 mm' for 6 or 7 cards is an interpolation the data doesn't give.
to10: Add 'snug for the first week, then it settles' to a bullet or the line under the button, and test against a holdout instead of a before-and-after comparison.

strength: It reads the 2.2% vs 8.0% sunscreen gap correctly and gives sunscreen its own email built on the dusky-skin review, with a clean three-way quiz split in Email 2.
mistake: Email 5 sends every non-buyer the same three-product routine with the salicylic wash morning and night, which contradicts Email 2C's 'don't start with an acid' advice to dry and sensitive people; Email 1 also prints 'brightening', a word we avoid, even if only as a contrast.
to10: Branch Email 5 by skin concern, drop the banned word, and add a holdout plus the gross-profit value of a lift.

strength: It personalises from Email 1 onward and keeps every email consistent with the quiz branch, so dry or sensitive people never get an acid. It adds smart Klaviyo logic (entry filter, cart pause, WhatsApp only to non-clickers), and every number checks out: ₹48 vs ₹9 per click, the 940-person holdout, and ₹32,900 per point of lift.
mistake: Paise-level prices like ₹628.20 read awkwardly in a calm brand email, and the projections stop at revenue rather than gross profit.
to10: Round prices to whole rupees, show the profit value net of the 10% code, and have Email 1 introduce the 'what's inside, and how much' promise so the brand's story lands on day 0.

strength: It gives Monsoon Dark buyers their own track, with a draft that names the blend and the roasters' closest match, and it holds ex-subscribers behind a 93% on-time gate, so it treats the real reasons people left rather than reaching for discounts.
mistake: It leads with the 91 to 180 day group and handles the 9,000 slipping 46 to 90 day buyers only as a side day-28 nudge, leaving the cheapest group to win back out of the waves and out of the value sum.
to10: Make the 46 to 90 day group wave one with a no-discount reminder, size its value, and back the 70% reachable figure with real email and WhatsApp overlap data.

strength: Its order follows the data: slipping 46 to 90 day buyers first with no code, Monsoon Dark next, and ex-subscribers gated on delivery and date choice. Its contacted counts, ₹385 at the 15% cap and 13%-weighted ₹535 for subscribers all check out.
mistake: The Monsoon Dark first email asks for a quiz instead of naming the closest match, and the 365+ day group gets 15% off in a single email with no test of whether that discount pays.
to10: Name the recommended match in the Monsoon Dark email, put the quiz second, and test the 365+ day offer at 0% against 15% before rolling it out.

strength: A clean, readable diagnosis with correct numbers: Meta explains the blended rise ($79 vs $104), first orders lose $33, and Meta customers lose $27 even over 18 months, with each check owned and dated.
mistake: Impact is mostly sized as High, Medium or Low rather than in contribution points, so the ranking and the week-13 targets aren't tied to a quantified margin goal.
to10: Size each move in contribution-margin points against a stated baseline, and give kill lines at week 4 and week 8 so I know when to stop.

strength: It turns the board's ask into a number: contribution after ads fell from 13.6% to 7.8%, worked out from the data. Each move is sized in margin points with low, likely and high cases, the arithmetic checks out (2.9 points from Meta, 0.9 from linen), and each has week-4 and week-8 kill lines.
mistake: The dense math reads above grade 8, and it leans on an unsourced 'about half' benchmark for flow revenue.
to10: Simplify the sizing prose so a non-analyst on the team can follow it, and replace the flow benchmark with the store's own pre-January flow revenue.

strength: The bundle maths checks out: ₹537 vs ₹572, +₹61 and +₹150 per step-up, with break-even counts. It also explains why a ₹849 duo would only discount 1,033 orders a month that already happen.
mistake: It says ₹599 touches only about 6% of orders (~1,000 a month). The ₹500 to 699 band is 27%, so about 13% (~2,300) sit between ₹499 and ₹598. That understates the risk behind its main threshold recommendation, and it never makes a COD-specific move against the 29% RTO.
to10: Size the ₹499 to ₹598 slice from the 27% band, build COD and RTO into the threshold choice (a COD fee or a different bar for prepaid), and turn lip balm into a cart add-on rather than a discounted main bundle.

strength: It ties the threshold to the RTO cliff at ₹500 and sizes the order bands correctly (2,320 at ₹599, 4,650 at ₹699). It then puts the money where the leak is: a lip balm cart add-on for orders under ₹499 and a COD fee test, with RTO counted at −₹130 in the main measure.
mistake: It keeps ₹499 but still tests ₹699, which mostly threatens the serum reorder it says it wants to protect. It also turns the proven face wash + serum pair into a trio instead of testing a plain routine duo.
to10: Test ₹699 for prepaid only, or drop that test in favour of the COD fee, and trial a face wash + serum duo against the trio.

strength: It ranks the in-app pop-up bug first with correct money (about 558 orders, ₹17 to ₹34 lakh a month), and its sample-size maths checks out for every test: 9.9% on 0.70%, 6.3% on 4.0% mobile add to cart, 5.5% on 4.4% add to cart. Each test also carries a gross-profit value.
mistake: It invents calendar dates (16 November to 17 January) the brief never gave, and it never gives firmness, the 19% chat topic, its own test. Firmness is only folded into the reviews tabs.
to10: Add a plain-words firmness module (with the 100-night line) as a test or a ship, and drop the made-up calendar in favour of week numbers.

strength: The browser-split funnel table is accurate and diagnostic: 3.7% vs 4.2% add to cart, 24% vs 53% cart to checkout. It ties the 4,300 errors to the 4,800 lost in-app carts and adds tracking events, an A/A test and a firmness test.
mistake: Test 5 bundles the hero image and the reviews move, so a win or loss can't be attributed to either change. Placeholders for the firmness rating and EMI amount leave homework.
to10: Split test 5 into its two changes, and put the gross-profit value of each test's smallest detectable effect beside it.

strength: The numbers are tight and correct throughout: ₹11.3 lakh RTO, 3,050 Tier 3 refusals, ₹45k per RTO point, and an 18,000-cart sizing. It also adds a practical 2 pm to midnight agent shift for the evening wave.
mistake: The prepaid nudge (template 3) is filed as Utility even though it persuades the buyer to switch payment. Meta will likely recategorise it, and the nudge isn't stronger for Tier 3, where half the RTO cost sits.
to10: Make the prepaid nudge a Marketing template with a tier-scaled incentive, and take a firmer Tier 3 stance (call plus cancel, or a small advance) from day one instead of easing it in.

strength: The flow is properly tiered by RTO risk. Expected loss per COD order (₹70 / ₹41 / ₹27) sets the prepaid discount for each band, Tier 3 gets calls and a 48-hour cancel, and repeat buyers skip confirmation. It also tests a ₹99 UPI advance against a holdout.
mistake: T1 waits 15 minutes and includes an expected delivery range, which adds a promise surface. It also states the prepaid discount amounts without checking them against margin beyond the RTO loss.
to10: Send T1 within 2 minutes, add an evening agent shift alongside the night menu, and state the exchange window explicitly in the size and exchange scripts.

strength: It catches the three big money signals: relaunch the paused creator winner, cut the COD-trap Starter Kit, and split Women 25-34 instead of killing the whole women's razor line.

to10: Make the Shopify-adjusted profit line the primary budget gate, add the exact Starter Kit fix conditions if it ever comes back, and tighten a couple of thresholds like the ₹800 no-purchase rule.

strength: It is disciplined on contribution after COD/RTO and clearly identifies the paused ASC winner, Women 25-34, and Starter Kit COD trap.

to10: Use the given 72% Shopify/Meta gap as the main conservative read, remove the invented date and extra experiment complexity, and make the budget calls less contradictory, especially the UGC increase while saying no ad set earns a raise.

strength: It is built around the actual winning signal: problem-first, on-feet worker creative, with the nurse and server Spark Ads live from day one and a $38 90-day payback target.

strength: It has the strongest measurement plan, using Shopify tags, post-purchase survey, blended lift, and a proposed state holdout instead of trusting TikTok ROAS.

to10: Add a fuller creator production plan around nurses, servers, warehouse, retail and teachers, and make all scale rules tie cleanly to the $38 90-day contribution target.

strength: It builds directly from the real signals: underfunded women 25-40, work flyers skipping the belt, and the unused quiet-wheels review theme.
mistake: A couple of concepts are still fairly conventional static proof ads, especially the gate and gift executions.
to10: Make every concept as visually distinctive as the 5 am sound test and tighten a few customer-facing lines for even more understated Mokobara polish.

strength: It reads the data well and gives distinct, usable angles led by belt-skipping, women lifting alone, and quiet wheels.
mistake: Some customer-facing claims and execution notes need tightening, especially 'No rattle', the cabin-sizer/dimensions idea, and the very low ₹4,500 cut threshold.
to10: Keep the same structure but make the copy fully launch-safe, add the missing price/spec discipline to more ads, and give cleaner test rules by concept and audience.

strength: It turns the actual signals into shootable ads: taste-test first, the 3 pm habit, price handled plainly, family/flavour angle, and paid disclosure built in.

strength: It is clean, shootable, on-brand, and correctly leads with the winning taste-test and swap formats instead of label reading.

to10: Add first-frame/on-camera ad disclosure, make the price objection more explicit in at least the taste-test or family script, and tighten the child/family claims with 'if true' guidance.

strength: It correctly brings back the paused front-of-pack winner, adds the missing taste hook from reviews, and leads the launch plan with those two highest-signal angles.

strength: It uses the strongest signals well: relaunches the tired winner, tests taste in customer words, and tackles the ₹90 objection directly.

to10: Keep the strong copy and launch choices, but trim the invented test setup or clearly separate it as optional so the deliverable stays copy-led.

strength: It leads with the real buying and return drivers: 5 to 12 cards, about 10 flat notes, 10/14 mm thickness, small coin pouch, and first-week snugness.

strength: It handles the main objections plainly above the fold, especially cash capacity, card break-in and who should choose a larger wallet.

strength: It correctly builds the flow around the main signals: dark spots lead, beginners need a slow-start plan, and sunscreen needs white-cast and stickiness objections answered.

strength: It is sharply built from the data, especially the niacinamide/dark-spots opportunity, the sunscreen conversion leak, and the beginner fear of actives.

strength: It correctly spots that discounts are not the main fix, gives Monsoon Dark and ex-subscriber tracks, and works from the right ₹557 gross profit per order.

strength: It cleanly identifies the real slowdown drivers: Meta cost inflation, linen returns, and the switched-off email capture/flows, then turns them into specific stop-do and week-one actions.

strength: It adds useful financial modelling, including contribution after ads, paid spend as a share of revenue, and a fresh swatch-kit test tied to Sarah's objection.

strength: It works the bundle economics clearly, especially the cannibalisation risk of discounting pairs customers already buy.

to10: Add a COD/prepaid-specific shipping recommendation and verify the ₹499-₹598 order volume before recommending the ₹599 line.

strength: It spots the real money leak in low-value COD orders and treats lip balm as the right cart add-on rather than a main discounted bundle.

strength: It catches the in-app checkout bug as a no-test fix, sizes the upside correctly at about 560 orders and ₹34 lakh gross margin a month, and builds the tests around the real objections: delivery, size, firmness, EMI and trust.

strength: It gives the owner the right first move immediately: fix the in-app checkout bug before testing, with the key browser split, order upside and gross-profit range shown plainly.

strength: It spots the two big levers: Tier 3 RTO cost and order-status chat load, then adds confirmation, shipped and delivery-day flows with sensible timing.

strength: It uses the owner’s data sharply: Tier 3 gets the harder confirm/call/cancel path, order-status chats get shipped/OFD templates, and every key flow has a holdout or net-profit check.

to10: Add the exact exchange-window wording, make the discount/advance test a clearly approved assumption, and ensure the mixed template buttons are supported by the provider before submission.

strength: It catches the three big account signals the owner cares about: relaunch the paused ASC winner, stop treating Women Body Razor as one average, and cut the Starter Kit COD trap with clear rupee logic.

to10: Tighten the contribution math by ad set, especially Starter Kit and the account-level 'safe line', while keeping the same clear budget calls and daily rules.

strength: It is disciplined about not scaling a losing account and gives a usable reserve-release system with concrete operating rules.

strength: It turns the actual signals in your data into a Monday-ready plan: on-feet worker Spark Ads first, problem-first hooks, proper Shopify/TikTok tracking, phased budget, and a day-30 decision tied to the 90-day economics.

strength: It gets the big strategic calls mostly right: problem-first over mission or discount, real on-feet creators over studio product shots, and a sensible tracking checklist before spend.

to10: Rework the budget and decision rules around the true 90-day break-even read, keep structure simpler in month one, and tie every scale/kill call to Shopify-verified new-customer economics rather than platform and before-vs-after shortcuts.

strength: It reads the audience and review data well, especially the under-served women 25 to 40 segment and the unused quiet-wheels proof, then turns those into distinct, usable concepts.

to10: Tighten any risky copy claims, keep every primary text strictly customer-facing, and make each concept's single test variable even cleaner.

strength: It is tightly built around the real signals in the brief—quiet wheels, women solo travellers, belt-skip for work flyers—and adds useful guardrails on scratches, front-pocket expectation, formats and claim handling.

strength: It reads the data correctly and turns the key signals into three distinct, ready-to-shoot scripts built around taste-first openings, the 3 pm habit, and price handling.

strength: It clearly uses the store's performance data to choose taste-first openings and handles the $3-per-can objection on camera instead of dodging it.

strength: It brings back the paused transparency winner, adds the missing taste angle from reviews, and gives a tight first-4 launch plan tied to what each ad is testing.
