to10: Tighten the copy set further around brand voice and use more owner-delighting display limits by keeping headlines closer to 40 and descriptions closer to 30 while making the launch plan even more execution-ready.

strength: It clearly sees the three key signals: relaunch transparency, test taste, and handle price honestly with genuinely different angles.

to10: Remove the made-up media plan details, stick to the approved brief, and keep the output focused on launch-ready copy plus the four combinations and what each tests.

strength: It directly tackles the real return drivers with precise cash and thickness numbers, honest trade-offs, and a clear break-in expectation.

to10: Remove the extra internal analysis, tighten the page to only the requested assets, and use the add-to-cart line to set the snug-first-week expectation.

strength: It is clear, on-brand, and does a good job of calmly explaining the cash and break-in trade-offs in customer language.

strength: It follows the main signals in the data well: leads with dark spots, gives sunscreen its own objection-handling email, and repeatedly teaches a slow start for beginners.

strength: It isolates the real drivers the data proves—Meta acquisition costs, switched-off CRM capture/flows, and linen returns—and turns them into an ordered plan with owners, stop rules, first steps, and a usable scorecard.

strength: It spots the real profit leak in low-value COD orders and ties bundles, threshold logic and testing back to shipping and RTO economics.

strength: It gives a clear, usable bundle ladder in the brand's voice and smartly protects the serum reorder from a risky ₹699 threshold jump.

strength: It spots the in-app checkout bug as the real blocker, quantifies the missed checkouts and orders, and ranks the next tests around the actual customer questions and page gaps.

strength: It does the owner-critical thing first: calls the in-app checkout issue a ship-now bug, sizes the upside correctly in money terms, and then gives a ranked test plan tied tightly to the evidence in the brief.

strength: It ties the flows to the real pain points in your data, especially Tier 3 COD risk and the missing shipment updates that drive status chats.

strength: It is sharper on tiered risk handling, holdouts, and the money logic by pincode group, and it directly addresses the order-status chat burden.

mistake: The parallel test lanes and fixed calendar dates could confuse attribution unless the team is comfortable reading interactions and the actual start date is reset.
to10: Make the schedule relative to launch date and simplify the test sequencing or spell out the factorial readout more plainly.

strength: It clearly diagnoses the in-app browser checkout break, gives the right gross margin upside, and uses honest sample-size expectations.
mistake: Some tests are less ready to run because they use placeholders or bundled changes, and the size test uses orders as the main metric, making it slower and less sensitive than needed.
to10: Replace placeholders with finished copy, separate bundled creative changes, and use add-to-cart or size-selection as the main metric where that better matches the page problem.

strength: It catches the big RTO and chat-load signals, adds shipping/OFD updates, after-hours automation, and gives usable Snitch-style templates and flows.
mistake: The prepaid switch is submitted as Utility with a payment CTA and no real incentive, and the payment URL variable is wrong, which could cause review or implementation issues.
to10: Make the prepaid nudge a Marketing template with a tiered incentive or advance test, fix the variable mapping, and tighten the tier-3 hold/call rules around the ₹5.5 lakh RTO problem.

strength: It targets the real profit leak—Tier 3 COD refusals—with differentiated flows, incentives sized below expected RTO loss, holdouts, and order-status automation.
mistake: A couple of Utility templates have borderline CTAs such as 'Order again', and the assumed prepaid discounts would need margin approval before launch.
to10: Remove any borderline marketing CTA from Utility templates and add exact margin guardrails for the ₹20/₹40 prepaid incentive and ₹99 advance test.

strength: It puts a rupee verdict on every ad set (Store profit column) and leads with the cheapest fix — reviving the paused 'Dad's razor' video — with the exact week-by-week cost-per-purchase evidence.
mistake: The launch-date framing ('14 to 27 November', 'Saturday 14 November') is invented and will look wrong if the owner runs this any other week; and the 86% attribution haircut for prospecting is asserted with no source, which quietly inflates the prospecting break-evens.
to10: Drop invented dates, show one worked example of the attribution haircut, and make the bolder retargeting holdout the headline move rather than an appendix.

strength: Twin safe/break-even lines per ad set make the attribution risk usable at a glance, and the copy cues ('No razor burn after a week', 'Finally not a flimsy pink razor') are on-voice and ready to shoot.
mistake: It scales Catalog DPA 20% and holds Retargeting on Meta's own 37%/-17% COD numbers without applying the heavier attribution haircut it itself says retargeting needs — a ₹38,000-and-₹40,000 decision resting on numbers the brief warns are inflated.
to10: Apply the retargeting/DPA attribution haircut consistently before scaling them, and show the arithmetic behind each break-even line rather than just the total.

strength: Built every rule off the owner's own money math and data: problem-first hooks, on-feet creators, Spark Ads from day one, and a $38 day-30 bar tied to 90-day break-even.
mistake: The budget table's stated reserve ($1,000) sits outside the phase rows, so a reader has to trust the total; and 33 ads in 30 days may be more creative than the team can actually produce.
to10: Show the budget table adding cleanly to $30,000 including the reserve and confirm the creative team's real weekly capacity for 15+6 ads.

strength: The three independent reads (store tags, survey, blended lift) plus a matched-state holdout is the sharpest day-30 measurement design of the two, and it correctly holds spend until the pixel is proven.
mistake: The zero-spend days 1 to 3 and lighter creative volume are sensible, but the dense tables and the holdout add complexity that could slow a team on Monday, and the 25+ targeting drops Maria/Tasha-adjacent younger buyers without saying why.
to10: Simplify the measurement section to one page and justify the 25+ age cut so the team isn't guessing.

strength: Concepts are genuinely distinct and every hook is lifted from real review or survey language, with the scratch risk handled up front and the first-three pick justified by cost per purchase.
mistake: The concept 4 test budget uses a blended ₹1,515 cost while concept 3 uses ₹1,058, so the three test budgets and the 'tenth of spend' claim don't quite reconcile with the broader 396-purchase base.
to10: Tighten the test-budget maths so each concept's spend figure and pass/stop rule trace to the same audience cost, and name the winner threshold explicitly.

strength: The reading of the numbers is sharp, including the women-25-40 purchase share and a direct test of the current colour-background style, and the 'check your airline's limit' caveat is exactly the right hedge.
mistake: The three concept hooks are close cousins of each other and of current ads (belt, lift, quiet), and concept 2's 'will it pass the gate check?' hook edges toward implying a guarantee the brand forbids.
to10: Push two of the eight concepts into angles the data doesn't already suggest (a gift-occasion story, a colour-scratch honesty angle) and give each a single test variable with a stated budget.

strength: It reads the paid-video data properly (taste-test $26 beats label $44) and builds all three scripts on that plus the real comment themes, with the 3 pm hook, the $3-a-can answer and the kids hook pulled straight from Dana and Marcus's words.
mistake: The 3 pm script's price line ('12 afternoons for me') is a bit soft and one hook ('$3 a can for a soda? Here's my honest take') drifts toward the defensive, plus the test-plan projections add extra balls the brief didn't ask for and dilute the finished scripts.
to10: Tighten the price rebuttal in Script 2 to a concrete comparison (a $5 coffee-shop drink) and keep the whole thing under 1,300 words by trimming the test plan.

strength: Clean, fast, shootable scripts with good hook alternates (the 2:59 clock, the mid-sip start) and disclosure baked in, and it correctly keeps the label after the taste moment.
mistake: It gives the blind-test reveal an odd 'pull a can from behind her back' staging and lets Script 3's claims land on the dad reading the label, which is the losing format, so it edges closer to the label-led trap than it should; it also has no in-script price answer beyond 'it's my one soda of the day'.
to10: Make Script 3 earn its family angle without a label read from Dad, and give the price objection a real on-camera answer in more than one script.

strength: It reads the paused 'flip the pack' winner correctly, brings it back with fresh words first, and makes the untested taste reviews (26% of reviews) a real launch test in the customer's own voice.
mistake: The stated display limits are wrong (headline 27, description 27 instead of about 40 and 30), so the character-count discipline the owner asked for is built on a bad rule and leaves room unused.
to10: Use the right Meta limits, add the taste quote to a headline, and show the money math behind the ₹210/₹290 bar-to-beat so the first-4 plan lands with a budget figure.

strength: Lines sound exactly like the brand and the buyers — 'minus the samosa', 'Save yourself the flip', 'Fair. Here's your ₹90' — and the launch plan includes a live-ad control, a budget, an early-cut rule and a day-14 read.
mistake: It adds test budget and a 5-cell plan the brief did not give, so some of the launch mechanics are invention the owner must approve.
to10: Keep the copy and plan, but flag the ₹6,000/day and ₹6,333/day figures as assumptions drawn from the brief so the owner can swap in real numbers without rework.

strength: The copy treats cash capacity and the break-in as honest, numbered facts, killing the top two return drivers while keeping the calm Bellroy voice.
mistake: The 'How to tell it worked' and assumptions sections pad a finished page, and the front-pocket answer is weaker than it could be without width and height.
to10: Add the outer dimensions or a clearer front-pocket verdict so the 24% of askers get a straight yes or no.

strength: It writes the cash and break-in trade-offs into the bullets, the description and the FAQ, and the 'What doesn't fit' list is a trust-builder a customer will feel.
mistake: It invents an extra-note capacity for the hidden pocket and a 'back pocket or jacket' claim that contradict the stated total, which is exactly the kind of overstatement that raises returns.
to10: Keep one consistent cash number across every section and remove the invented hidden-pocket and back-pocket claims.

strength: Connects each email to a specific number in the data and answers the sunscreen chat fears with the actual review line, while keeping the calm labelled-strength voice.
mistake: Email 5 mixes the 'two-step routines' with a single active plus sunscreen but presents sunscreen as a step for oily skin in a way that subtly contradicts Email 2's 'one product' logic, and the ₹48/₹9 per-click figures, while roughly right, are not shown with working.
to10: Show the per-click and code-value arithmetic explicitly and tighten Email 5 so the routine logic matches the earlier branch.

strength: Warm, plain-spoken emails with a strong quiz-conditional structure that speaks to Sneha's and Arjun's words and keeps each email to one job.
mistake: Email 5's '3-step routine' pushes all three products and a ₹1,297 bundle, which contradicts the brand's start-slow, one-active message and risks irritation for beginners; it also assumes a code expiry date placeholder without giving the working.
to10: Replace the three-product bundle in the final email with a single matched product plus sunscreen and keep the start-slow promise consistent to the end.

strength: It reads the data the way the owner does: the Monsoon Dark track, the ex-subscriber delivery gate, and starting with the 46-90 day 'slipping' band are all handled with the right offer logic and the maths shown.
mistake: A few arithmetic or consistency slips: 'a buyer is lapsed at 68' is unexplained, and G1's reachable math (8,060 × 62% = 4,997, not 4,497) affects the profit projection.
to10: Reconcile every reachable and profit figure to a single worked sheet and drop the cryptic 'lapsed at 68' line.

strength: Strong, warm message drafts that name the coffee and the farm, and a sharp point that the day-28 nudge is the cheapest fix for the repeat-rate fall.
mistake: It starts with the 91-180 day band instead of the cheaper 46-90 day at-risk group, and its profit table leans on assumed 2-order repeats rather than the owner's per-order gross profit, which inflates the number.
to10: Put the 46-90 day slipping group first with a no-discount reminder, and rebuild the worth table from ₹557/₹442/₹385 per order with the working shown.

strength: Separates proved from to-check cleanly and ranks the real money leaks (Meta/linen, switched-off flows) with owners and first-week steps.
mistake: The payback math ($94 LTV) bakes in assumptions that aren't stress-tested, and the comforter 'too warm' fix is thin; expected order is slightly loose.
to10: Tighten the repeat-value assumption with an actual repeat order value and margin, and quantify each move's gross profit in dollars rather than vague 'medium/high' bands.

strength: Puts every move in one unit (points of contribution margin) with sizing, lines and stop thresholds, plus a genuinely fresh swatch-kit concept and a sharp brand catch on the 'hotel' line.
mistake: The contribution baseline (7.8% vs 13.6%) is built on an unstated, fragile solver (w × −11% + (1−w) × 6% = −4%) and stacked assumptions; a couple of projections (5.6-point swatch upside) look optimistic.
to10: Show the baseline working plainly and flag it as an estimate, and trim the optimistic range on the swatch test so the numbers hold up under scrutiny.

strength: Builds a clear price ladder from the real top pair and picks ₹599 with worked profit-per-order maths and break-evens per bundle.
mistake: The ₹599 band assumption (about 6% of orders, 1,000/month) is invented and the walk-away loss of ₹271 per order is not traceable to the data, so the +₹28,000 net is shaky.
to10: Show the ₹499–₹598 slice from the order export instead of assuming it and tie the walk-away loss to the stated ₹620 AOV gross profit.

strength: It reads the refusal cliff correctly, keeps ₹499, and puts the real money in the 6,880 sub-₹499 carts with a lip-balm lift and a COD fee test, all with break-evens and ranges.
mistake: The ₹699 projection range (−₹0.72 to +₹2.35 lakh) is very wide and the band shares (2,320 and 4,650 orders) are asserted rather than shown from the order spread.
to10: Show the band arithmetic for ₹599 and ₹699 orders from the stated spread and tighten the ranges so the owner can trust the decision.

strength: Puts the in-app checkout bug first with the money sized, then ranks five tests by expected impact with honest detectable effects that respect the 0.56% mobile conversion reality.
mistake: The hero image test ranks last but still carries a projected ₹5.9 lakh gain on the thinnest evidence, which slightly overstates its value against the delivery and size tests.
to10: Trim the hedgey projections on the weakest test and add a one-line sample-size sanity check for the 4-week all-device tests to prove the 9.9% effect is reachable in the traffic.

strength: The funnel table by browser is a sharp, honest read that names the in-app checkout bug with the near-exact error-to-drop-off match.
mistake: It spends one of only five test slots on a combined image-and-reviews test rather than isolating the highest-confidence page change, and it leaves EMI amounts and firmness ratings as fill-in blanks, so it is not ready to run.
to10: Split the image and reviews into separate, ranked tests or drop the image test for an isolated reviews move, and fill the EMI and firmness numbers so the page copy can ship as written.

strength: RTO cost is split by pincode group with per-order refusal math that justifies tiered discounts and calls, and the holdout is built in.
mistake: T4 (prepaid switch) is submitted as Marketing but the body carries a ₹20/₹40 discount that only works after Confirm, which risks Meta rejecting or recategorising it, and the discount is never sized against margin.
to10: Make the prepaid and cart templates clean Marketing with the incentive properly sized and the STOP footer on every template, and put the after-hours bot menu live before chats are rerouted.

strength: The reply scripts are the most usable part: short, light Hinglish, and clearly mapped to the five real questions with an after-hours menu.
mistake: Template 3 is filed as Utility but tries to switch COD buyers to prepaid with a UPI link, which is Marketing and will be recategorised or rejected, and the 7-day exchange claim is stated as fact without the store's real policy.
to10: Get the categories right (template 3 as Marketing, template 1 as Utility without any payment link), make the exchange wording an assumption rather than a fact, and show the money behind each move like Output 1 does.

strength: The opening picks and the spend rules are built on my numbers: women at ₹1,058 on 18% of spend, 15 purchases per concept at ₹24k/₹16k/₹23k, total ₹63k, with a stop rule, and it also kills the scratch claim and the missing front pocket before they happen.
mistake: Concepts 6, 8 and partly 7 fall back on the big-type-on-clean-colour static the owner is tired of, and their test definitions are vague ('whether the top review theme sells broad') rather than a single measurable variable.
to10: Give the last three concepts the same scene-level visual detail and one clear test variable each as the first four.

strength: Every concept is complete to the same template, and the set has the freshest single idea in either answer: the cabin-sizer demo that answers Karan's gate-check worry head-on, plus the 26%-of-purchases read and the '63 more purchases' illustration, which are all arithmetically right.
mistake: Its running rule ('three times blended cost per purchase, about ₹4,500') would have me cutting or scaling on roughly three purchases, and it then puts three segment-specific concepts in one broad campaign with no budget split, losing the audience learning its own opening sets up.
to10: Replace the read rule with a purchase count that can survive noise and give each concept its own cell, budget and stop number.

strength: Clean, shootable scripts that correctly put taste first and handle the $3-a-can price objection inside Script 2.
mistake: It applies the CPA table but never surfaces the real insight — that $24,000 went to the worst-opening style — and its test plan has no budgets or cut/scale rules to act on.
to10: Show the money (spend vs CPA misallocation, the pack-price working) and give a concrete test plan with numbers to keep, cut or scale each hook.

strength: It names that $24,000 went to the $44 label opener, reframes the price as '$35.99 ÷ 12 = 12 afternoons,' and backs it with a real test plan with budgets and cut/scale rules.
mistake: It sets a scale target near the $26 taste-test CPA without tying the breakeven to gross profit per order (COGS is unknown), so the profitability ceiling is asserted, not proven.
to10: Add the gross-profit-per-order ceiling (AOV $35.99 minus product cost, shipping and fees) so the '$26 scale' and '$32 keep' lines are shown to be profitable, not just better than the old benchmark.

strength: It does exactly what I asked with my own numbers: six truly different angles in my voice, the paused ₹210 front-of-pack winner brought back first, taste and the ₹90 objection tested, with a launch plan I can hand to a media buyer tomorrow (budget, cell size, kill rule, UTM tracking).
mistake: The test is spread thin: five cells at ₹1,200 a day gets about four purchases a day per cell, which is below Meta's 50-a-week learning phase, and 58 purchases is a shaky read on a 20% difference.
to10: Consolidate into fewer, better-funded cells (or run the copy test on one ad set) so each cell clears the learning phase, and name which live ad to switch off when D wins.

strength: The test thinking is sharper than mine: comparing front-of-pack as a fact (A) against the same truth written as 'you' (C) is a genuinely new read, holding P4 back because it teaches nothing next to the live ₹290 ad is disciplined, and the legal fallback for quoting reviews shows it thought about what I'd actually be allowed to run.
mistake: Two of the six primary texts (P1 and P5) are the same front-of-pack angle reworded, which breaks the 'each a different angle' brief, and the launch plan has no budget, cell size or kill rules, so I still have homework before it runs.
to10: Give me six genuinely separate angles (add a gym/protein text for Aditya and keep one 4pm text) and put real money, sample size and an early-cut number behind the four launch cells.

strength: Every number that drives the return problem is above the fold and in plain words — about 10 flat notes, 10 mm with 6 cards, snug slots for a week — and the copy names the trade-off in the brand's calm voice.
mistake: It builds the money answer on an invented capacity (hidden pocket takes one extra note) that pushes capacity up rather than down, which is the exact direction that feeds the 'holds less cash than expected' return it is meant to cut.
to10: Hold capacity to the proven 10 flat notes with no extra, and add a way to prove the change worked (cash-return rate and card-slot returns by order date, with conversion as the guardrail).

strength: It answers the returns problem and proves it: conservative cash figure, break-in expectation in three places, wrong-fit buyers routed to other wallets so the sale is kept rather than lost, and a measurement plan with correct baseline arithmetic (3.3 and 1.0 per 100 orders) and a guardrail.
mistake: The 'what fits' example invents a thickness the brief never gives — about 10 to 11 mm for 6 or 7 cards — where the data only supports 10 mm at 6 and 14 mm at 12.
to10: Stamp the break-in easing note into the above-the-fold bullets and the line under the button, and give thickness only for the card counts the data actually states.

strength: It builds the whole series on the signals that matter — 44%/55% dark-spots branch, the 61% beginner fear, and the sunscreen's 2.2% click-to-order answered with the 'No white cast, even on my dusky skin' review — and the emails are written out complete with greeting, sign-off, CTA and links, so they can go into Klaviyo almost as they stand.
mistake: Email 5 gives everyone the same three-step routine with salicylic acid wash morning and night plus niacinamide at night, which contradicts the brand's own 'one new active at a time, start every other night' rule and ignores the quiz branch in the highest-intent email; it also invents the 'two thin layers instead of one thick one' sunscreen instruction and gives no holdout or lift maths.
to10: Branch Email 5 by skin concern with one active plus sunscreen and correct per-branch prices, and add a holdout plan showing what one extra point of 14-day orders is worth in rupees.

strength: It translates the data into money per click (₹48 for niacinamide vs ₹9 for sunscreen), branches the final email into three concern-specific routines with exact prices (₹698/₹628.20, ₹998/₹898.20, ₹399/₹359.10), quotes Sneha and Arjun in their own words, and adds a 60-day holdout with correct lift maths (about 940 people, about ₹32,900 per point).
mistake: The body copy is thinner than a finished welcome letter — no greeting, no sign-off, and the footer given as a spec rather than copy — and Email 4 'read the label' is a soft brand-education slot that points beginners at all three products, adding the choice load the series is meant to remove.
to10: Finish every email with a human opening and team sign-off and real footer copy, and swap Email 4 for a proof or social-proof email (the dusky-skin review, or the plain team photo) that still moves people to buy before the code ends.

strength: It works the groups in the order my data argues for, starting with the 9,000 at 46 to 90 days at no discount, then the 5,200 Monsoon Dark buyers, and it holds the ex-subscribers behind a hard delivery gate of 93% on-time for four weeks.
mistake: Two numbers are left hanging: the ₹4.2 to 8.6 lakh 12-month headline has no working behind it, and the ₹535 profit used for ex-subscribers doesn't match the 15% offer it gives some of them.
to10: Show the break-even lift per group in points (message cost plus discount over ₹385 to ₹557 margin) next to the projected range, so I can see at a glance which waves are worth sending even on a weak read.

strength: The day-28 running-low nudge attacks the leak before customers lapse, and the honest note that discounting people who would buy anyway costs about ₹70,000 shows real commercial thinking.
mistake: My 9,000 customers at 46 to 90 days, the cheapest group to bring back, are not in the target table with a size, offer and holdout, and group A is counted at 13,100 even though the assumptions say ex-subscribers are pulled out of every group.
to10: Put the 46 to 90 day group first as its own wave with a light no-discount message, a holdout and a value line, and make the group counts reconcile with the ex-subscriber carve-out.

strength: It isolates Meta as the cost driver ($121 vs $92 Google), shows the first order loses $33 and that a Meta customer never pays back at $94 lifetime value, and turns that into a simple, runnable $94 cap plus a linen pause.
mistake: The scorecard asks new customer orders to improve to -5% while the plan deliberately cuts paid spend and says to 'accept fewer new orders', and the '$23k to $41k' upside from cutting $100k of Meta spend is never explained.
to10: Bridge today's contribution margin to the day-90 number in one line of working, and set a new-customer order target that is consistent with cutting paid spend.

strength: It answers the board's actual ask by valuing everything in points of contribution margin (7.8% today, 12.9% at day 90) with the working shown, per-move effort scores, week-4/week-8 lines and a stop rule on each line, and it flags that Sarah's 'nice hotel' line would read as the banned hotel-quality claim.
mistake: Two sizing inputs are invented rather than sourced or ranged - the welcome flow 'earning about 1.8% of revenue' and the flow rebuild adding 2.75% of revenue when 22% x 11 points is 2.4% - and the plan is pinned to a specific 16 Nov 2026 start with Black Friday in week 2 that the brief never gave.
to10: Source or explicitly range the two pressure-tested inputs in moves 2 and 3, and lead with this week's three actions so the density does not bury them.

strength: Every number traces back to the brief and checks out — the funnel table, the 4,300 errors versus 4,800 in-app abandoned carts, the 1,860 extra checkouts, the 560 orders and ₹34 lakh margin, and the ₹1,209 no-cost EMI guide all reconcile exactly, with a clean 4-week sample-size calculation.
mistake: It makes orders per session the main metric for the mobile-only size test at a 12% detectable effect, so the most promising page fix sits on a 4-week read that will probably land flat, when add-to-cart with orders as guardrail would have answered it in two weeks.
to10: Use add-to-cart or checkout reach as the primary metric on the mobile-only, low-traffic tests with orders as a guardrail, and show the money each test is worth so the priority order has a rupee reason.

strength: It reads the traffic honestly — add-to-cart as the primary metric where orders per session could never reach significance, orders as guardrail, an explicit warning that small real lifts will read flat — and names the right segment per test (desktop for EMI, in-app versus other mobile for the hero), with a half-to-all range on the checkout fix instead of a single ceiling.
mistake: The per-test rupee projections are inconsistent: tests 2, 4 and 5 halve a relative effect that was computed on add-to-cart and then apply it to orders, giving an implausibly small ₹4.5 lakh for the size test, while test 1 does no halving at all.
to10: Apply one stated money method across all five tests so each detectable effect translates into a rupee figure the owner can compare, and give a single all-device read for the hero-image test rather than an underpowered sub-segment.

strength: It builds the flow around the pincode reality — expected refusal loss per COD order (₹70 Tier 3, ₹41 Tier 2, ₹27 Metro) with the prepaid discount sized below it — and still names the downside (confirmation cancels orders that might have delivered, discounts reach buyers who'd have paid) with holdouts to measure net.
mistake: It assumes checkout opt-in covers marketing cart messages and does not size the 30%-abandoned cart volume, so the cart case rests on a stated assumption rather than a number.
to10: Show the cart opportunity in rupees (carts reaching the shipping step, expected recovery, gross profit) and confirm the opt-in language the two Marketing cart templates depend on.

strength: It flags that checkout opt-in may cover only order updates, sends the prepaid nudge as a free-form chat inside the 24-hour window to save template cost, and quantifies the leverage cleanly — each 1% moved to prepaid removes ~63 RTOs (~₹11,000).
mistake: It drops the prepaid incentive the owner asked for and files the pay-online message as Utility, and it leaves the 7-day exchange policy as an assumption that appears in a template and two scripts, so a wrong policy would ship to customers.
to10: Deliver a Marketing prepaid offer sized below the expected refusal loss by pincode tier, and cover all five after-hours topics (including size and exchange) in the night menu instead of three buttons.

strength: Every ad set gets a rupee decision built on after-RTO, Shopify-adjusted economics, and it catches all three owner signals: relaunch the paused creator video, split women 25-34, cut the COD-trap Starter Kit.
mistake: The two-line 'safe ₹282 / break-even ₹394' framework double-counts the attribution gap on top of per-set RTO math and gets confusing (the Starter Kit break-even of ₹271 vs ₹194 is muddled), which risks a wrong pause/scale call.
to10: Clean one-number break-even per ad set (no parallel safe line) with the attribution haircut applied once and shown.

strength: Rigorous, traceable economics with a state-split holdout test for retargeting that genuinely answers whether retargeting pays, plus a reserve-released-by-rule budget that caps at ₹5,60,000.
mistake: Dense and over-engineered for a 'I want decisions, not reporting' owner; the holdout test and multiple probability assumptions add reading load, and holding the Starter Kit's COD issue while staying at ₹60,200 on Beard Kit and ₹56,000 on UGC is debatable.
to10: Cut the extra frameworks down to decisions and one clean budget table so the Monday actions jump off the page.

strength: Every concept is anchored to a real signal in the data — quiet wheels, women's cheaper CPA, belt-skip desire — with hooks lifted straight from review language.
mistake: The '₹292 a trip' and the '63 more purchases' uplift are illustrations without showing the division or flagging the assumption beyond a light touch, and concept 7's proof carousel risks showing a scuffed dark shell if shot carelessly.
to10: Show the arithmetic for every rupee figure (spend shares, per-trip maths, uplift) inline so nothing has to be trusted on faith.

strength: Tight, scannable table plus honest risk callouts (dark-shell scuffs, front-pocket gap, mute-viewer risk) make it easy to brief a team.
mistake: Concept 7 'Four specs' is a generic spec-demo that adds little range, and the ₹24,000/₹16,000/₹23,000 spend-per-concept test math is heavier and less clear than it needs to be for a first read.
to10: Replace the weakest spec-demo concept with a genuinely fresh angle and simplify the budget-per-test calculation to a single line.

strength: It resurrects the paused front-of-pack winner with fresh words, builds the taste angle straight from the 26% review phrase, and faces the ₹90-a-bar objection head-on, all in blunt brand voice.
mistake: The 27-character headline limit is more conservative than Meta's actual ~40, which is fine, but P4 ('Not even a little') repeats a line identical to a live ₹290 ad and is only parked, so the six are slightly less differentiated than claimed.
to10: Tighten the price/value angle so it reads as value rather than just repeating the objection, and add per-ad expected lift or kill rules with rupee targets.

strength: It pairs buyer-phrase headlines and copy (including 'Your 4 pm, minus the samosa') with a real test plan, a control cell, per-cell rupee maths and a 20% win rule that tells you exactly when to act.
mistake: It invents a ₹6,000/day test budget and ties ad C's success to retargeting without brief support, and the early-cut rule (₹1,140 with no purchase) is noisy at these cell sizes.
to10: Drop the invented budget and instead say how to size cells off actual traffic, and make the price ad lead with the ₹90 value rather than quoting the objection.

strength: Leads with real numbers (10 notes flat, 10/14 mm, 5-12 cards) and turns the cash and break-in return drivers into calm, honest page copy in Bellroy's voice.
mistake: Front-pocket FAQ hedges instead of answering the data's second-biggest question, and the assumption that the hidden pocket adds 'one extra note' risks overstating cash beyond the confirmed ~10.
to10: Answer the front-pocket question decisively with outer dimensions and drop the extra-note assumption so the cash figure never overstates capacity.

strength: Turns the data into a working plan: honest 'not for you' section, break-in note targeting the 7-day returns, and a measurement plan with baseline return figures and a conversion guardrail.

to10: Tie every thickness claim strictly to the brief's two known points and confirm outer dimensions so the front-pocket answer is definitive.

strength: Uses the real signals well: sunscreen leak explained and answered in a dedicated email, quiz branching into three product paths, and a slow-start email built for the 61% beginners.

to10: Tighten to the winning dark-spot path with stronger persona language from Sneha and Arjun, and replace vague product claims with exact, approved lines from the product pages.

strength: Fits the data and the people: matched product from quiz, evening send logic for a working Pune buyer, and a hard look at the sunscreen numbers that also names a test and what a lift is worth.

to10: Give Email 1 the welcome-and-code job only, put the product match in Email 2 as the first real teaching moment, and show the sign-up and lift arithmetic so the projection is checkable.

strength: Fixes the real causes first — a hard gate on ex-subscribers until on-time delivery hits 93%, a dedicated Monsoon Dark match track, and a day-28 'running low' nudge for Aarav-style drifters — with clean ₹557/₹442/₹385 working and a page of on-voice drafts.

strength: Correctly puts the slipping 46-90 day buyers first as a no-discount reminder, names the Monsoon Dark retirement at 29% of the 181-365 band, gates ex-subscribers on delivery, and adds a fresh pre-order-lot idea for Monsoon Dark fans.

to10: Drop or hold the 15% on the 365+ goodbye email and state a clear assumption on whether the Monsoon Dark beans can actually be re-sourced before making pre-order the group's plan.

strength: Kills the linen-on-Meta money leak with a hard $94 payback rule and fixes the switched-off flows in week one, both sized in margin points with owners.

strength: Plain, readable diagnosis with a clean proved-vs-check table and a clear 'stop advertising linen' call that a team could act on.
mistake: Moves are not ranked with real gross-profit numbers — impacts are vague ('high', 'medium') and the scorecard leaves contribution target as 'set baseline in week 1', which is homework for the owner.
to10: Put a working number on each move's gross-profit impact, rank by that, and give a contribution target instead of asking the owner to set one.

strength: Puts the top real pair (face wash + serum) first, protects the serum reorder against a ₹699 line, and builds the threshold math and COD/RTO leak into one coherent money story.

to10: Show one consistent break-even basis (either incremental vs. the current best single item or vs. existing pair buyers) and quantify the expected lift with a stated range, not just a break-even threshold.

strength: Sharpest idea in either answer: the serum-page price ladder (₹599 → ₹749 with lip balm → ₹999 routine) and the ₹599 threshold that still lets the serum ship free, plus the clear 'why not ₹699' reasoning.

to10: Rebuild every money number from one clean model with the actual ₹499–₹598 slice sourced rather than assumed, fix the internal inconsistencies in the serum + lip balm profit, and use the same break-even basis for the three bundles.

strength: Calls the in-app checkout bug first with the money sized (about ₹34 lakh gross margin a month) and ranks the five tests on real evidence, with honest sample-size maths.
mistake: The Test 1 and 3 detectable-effect figures (0.70% baseline, 10%) are slightly off the page's real mobile-weighted conversion and the firmness/EMI copy has blanks that need filling before launch.
to10: Replace the remaining placeholder figures (firmness rating, EMI amount, delivery dates) with real values and state the pooled conversion baseline explicitly so the detectable-effect maths is fully traceable.

strength: Leads with the bug and its money, ranks the five tests cleanly with per-test metrics, guardrails and sample maths, and adds a genuinely fresh bolder move of letting buyers pick a delivery day.
mistake: The fixed week-by-week calendar (ending 17 January) is brittle and some projected sales figures (₹4.5 lakh, ₹5.9 lakh) mix mobile and all-device baselines without showing the arithmetic, which is more likely to mislead than Output 1's cleaner maths.
to10: Show the arithmetic behind every projected rupee figure and drop the hard calendar for a simple sequencing rule so the plan survives a slipped start or a sale.

strength: Every rule is tied to our own money and our own data: the $38.46 90-day break-even, the $28.97 problem-first vs $50.85 mission-first hook costs, the 11.4s vs 2.8s watch times, and the March licence end all drive the plan.
mistake: It never names who owns creative and comments after set-up, and the 'creator brief' is only a hook table, so the creative lead still has homework on Monday.
to10: Add a named owner per workstream and a one-page creator brief sheet (shot list, do and don't, banned claims) so the team can hand it straight to creators.

strength: It reads easily and covers the whole job in plain words: set-up, structure, creative, budget, kill/scale, day-30 test, plus a Monday owner list.

to10: Replace the loose day-30 read with a store-tagged plus survey read that must agree, and tie every kill, scale and budget move to a dollar figure from our own data.

strength: Copy is genuinely in our voice — short, calm lines like 'Land. Roll. Leave.' — and it turns quiet wheels, belt-skipping and lift-it-alone into three separate shootable concepts with hooks pulled from real review lines.
mistake: Its test plan is too thin to judge anything: three times blended cost per purchase is about ₹4,500, roughly three purchases per concept, and running a women-specific concept inside one broad campaign muddles the very read it is asking for.

strength: It leads with the two awkward truths in my data — scuffs on dark shells and the missing front pocket — then hands my team sizes, safe zones, CTA, link, paid-partnership labelling, character-counted headlines and a ₹63,000 test budget with a 15-purchase rule.
mistake: Primary texts drift into spec-listing, so a few read denser than our 'short lines, grade 7' voice, and showing a real luggage-scale reading risks displaying a number that disagrees with 'about 2.6 kg'.

strength: Sharpest read of the store's own numbers: it names that the $24,000 label-read opener was the worst performer, builds all three scripts to open on taste, and adds a cut-rule test plan plus creator rights and deliverables.

to10: Put a one-line disclosure/deliverables header on each script and trim wording so it scans in seconds.

strength: Cleanest, most natural spoken scripts — hooks like "It's 3 pm. You know what that means." and beats like "And one for me" read aloud beautifully and stay on brand.

to10: Add an on-camera "Olipop paid me" line to each script and put deliverables, safe zones and rights into each creator brief.

strength: Brings the paused front-of-pack winner back with fresh words, leads with the unused taste reviews, and takes the ₹90 objection head-on with real customer quotes.

strength: Clean, tight copy set with honest character counts, a clear A-vs-C logic that isolates fact versus persona, and a sensible backup if review quotes are not allowed.
mistake: The launch rationale skips a direct taste-versus-transparency test by pairing P2 with H2, and describes limits as 27 for both headline and description, which narrows headlines unnecessarily.
to10: Use the correct headline (~40) and description (~30) limits, and set the first four so taste is tested head-to-head against the returning front-of-pack angle with a named money read.

strength: It puts the cash number above the fold and repeats it precisely ('about 10 notes, laid flat, in total, hidden pocket included') in the spec and FAQ, directly attacking the 44% return reason, then backs it with correct return-rate maths (about 3.3 and 1.0 per 100 orders) and a smart fallback if conversion drops.

to10: Move the snug-first-week expectation into the above-the-fold bullets and flag the 7-card thickness as an estimate, so every number on the page traces straight to the brief.

strength: It puts the break-in expectation in the first bullets ('slots start snug and ease in over about a week'), which targets the 21% 'too tight' cluster and the 63%-within-7-days pattern at the moment the buyer is deciding.

to10: Trim the SEO title under 60 characters and settle the hidden-pocket note count into one stated number so nothing needs confirming before it goes live.

strength: Built the series around the data: dark spots, sunscreen's click-to-order leak, and beginner fear, with segmented product paths and a clear holdout plan.

to10: Fix the WhatsApp to give product-specific usage, especially sunscreen every morning, and make every merge field exact for Klaviyo.

strength: Clear, calm copy and a strong sunscreen FAQ that uses the white-cast review and answers the three chat questions.

to10: Segment Email 5 and keep the safe one-product start, remove 'brightening', and add exact send times.

strength: It ranks the 46-90 day 'at risk' group first with no discount, gives Monsoon Dark its own match track, gates ex-subscribers behind a delivery fix, and works everything off the correct ₹557 per-order profit with discount-adjusted figures (₹442, ₹385).

to10: Add the exact break-even lift per group and explain the ex-subscriber profit figure.

strength: Strong explicit reasoning — why A and B start with no discount, a stated 1.5-point break-even lift, and a fix mapped to each subscription cancel reason (late, too much, price, moving).

strength: Builds a coherent, internally consistent contribution-margin story (7.8% today to 12.9% target) with per-move sizing, owners, stops and a runnable numeric scorecard that a team could start Monday.

strength: A clean, honest proved-versus-needs-checking table with owners and check-by dates, and plain-language moves a small team can follow.

strength: It prices each tier's prepaid discount below the loss it removes (₹40 vs ₹70 in Tier 3, ₹20 vs ₹41 in Tier 2, nothing in Metro) and proves it with a Tier 3 holdout.

strength: Built entirely on our own signals: the on-feet creator watch times, the Meta hook cost table, the $27.10 first-order and ~$38 90-day break-even, with kill and scale rules in dollars and a day-3 tracking gate.

strength: Clear, readable structure with a usable weekly refresh rule and a sensible 'own the rights before March' note.

strength: It ties every script back to the numbers ($26 vs $44 vs $32 per purchase, $35.99÷12=$3) and builds a real test plan with cut rules, plus the on-screen 'Ad' and 'Olipop paid me' moments baked into each script.

strength: It catches every real signal in our data (the paused winner was tired not broken, taste reviews never run, the ₹90 objection) and builds the whole set and launch plan around them in our blunt voice.

strength: Copy is closest to our customers' actual words (samosa, chalky, gym bag) and the launch plan is unusually complete, with a real control ad, budget, sample-size logic and an early-cut rule.

to10: Keep the strong copy but shrink the plan to what was asked (4 launch combos and what each tests) and state the budget as an explicit optional assumption rather than the plan's backbone.

strength: It builds the whole page around the data's real leaks — cash capacity stated in notes above the fold, the break-in expectation in bullet, description and FAQ, and the '8 cards still closes flat' proof — in a calm, on-brand voice.
mistake: The hidden pocket is hedged ('about one extra flat note') while the FAQ and 'what fits' section imply it adds capacity, which risks re-creating the cash-expectation gap the page is meant to close.
to10: Settle the hidden-pocket capacity with one confirmed number and use it consistently, so no buyer counts an extra note that isn't there.

strength: It closes the cash ambiguity decisively ('about 10 notes in total, hidden pocket included'), sources every return reduction to a measured number, and adds a post-launch measurement plan the owner can run.

to10: Replace the invented 10–11 mm figure with a stated number or drop it, keeping every dimension traceable to the brief.

strength: Built the whole series on the real numbers: niacinamide at 8.0% click-to-order as the default pick, a dedicated email dismantling the white-cast and stickiness doubts behind the sunscreen's 2.2%, and a start-slow plan for the 61% new to actives.

strength: Warm, on-brand, plain-language copy with a clean code-and-how-we-label welcome that matches the Minimalist voice closely.

to10: Lead the series with the dark-spots routine people actually chose (44%) and the niacinamide winner (8%), then fix the sunscreen doubts earlier with the review as proof, and make every email paste-ready with a real code field and no 'check the product page' caveats.

strength: It catches and acts on every signal in the data: the Monsoon Dark gap gets its own named track, the courier problem gates the ex-subscriber win-back, and the at-risk 46-90 day group is worked first with no discount.

to10: Plain-text merge fields with a one-line note on what each field pulls, so the team can load the drafts into their email tool without touching the code.

strength: The offer logic is immediately usable and the reasoning about why a 10% discount costs ₹115 of a ₹557 order is clear enough for a non-expert to follow and defend to a founder.

to10: Show the break-even lift rate per group (the minimum lift needed to cover discounts and message costs) and drop the invented multi-order value assumption so the projection is conservative and defensible.

strength: A tight diagnosis that separates proved from to-check, with every number tracing to the brief, and moves ranked by gross profit and effort with clear owners and first steps.

strength: Genuinely fresh angles like the swatch kit and quantified upside ranges, with a clear contribution margin focus.
mistake: The weekly scorecard target for new customer orders ('Down 11% or better') is unclear and likely a mistake, and the plan is dense with jargon like 'points' and 'line' that could confuse a non-expert owner.
to10: Clarify the scorecard targets (e.g., set a realistic improvement like -5%), simplify the language, and ensure every projection is clearly tied to a simple assumption check.

strength: Nails the two signals that matter—the in-app checkout bug sized in gross profit (₹34 lakh/month) and the 81% four-size insight—and ranks delivery date and size first with honest traffic-aware sample maths.
mistake: The pop-up fix gain is presented as a clean ceiling without noting that in-app browsers may lose cookies/attribution, so the ₹34 lakh is optimistic and the test baselines may be polluted until the fix and tracking are live; also leaves firmness rating and EMI amounts as blanks.
to10: Show the working for each sample-size figure and flag the in-app attribution/cookie caveat beside the ₹34 lakh gain, so the owner can trust the numbers rather than adjust them.

strength: Treats the bug as a fix-first move with a ranged, honest ₹17–34 lakh projection, then sequences five tests in two lanes with dated windows, per-test smallest effects tied to real traffic, guardrails that include gross profit after EMI/COD costs, and a ship rule.

to10: Add the exact arithmetic behind the 9.9% and 6.3% detectable effects and a one-line cookie/attribution caveat for in-app traffic so the owner never has to re-derive a number.

strength: It builds a tiered COD-confirmation flow with calls and a 48-hour cancel rule aimed squarely at the Tier 3 band causing ~half the RTO cost, and prices each discount against the expected refusal loss it removes (₹70/₹41/₹27).

to10: Show the agent-minutes math proving the Tier 3 call volume fits the 4-person team, or cap calls to the highest-risk slice, and fix the second template category so no marketing content sits in Utility.

strength: Cleanest, most paste-ready set of templates with correct categories throughout, and a sharp operational fix: move one agent to a 2pm–midnight shift so the 31% after-hours wave gets a real person.

to10: Differentiate the confirmation and prepaid nudge by pincode risk with the RTO money worked out per band, and put the prepaid nudge incentive in a Marketing template so the switch actually happens.

to10: Using a bounded range for CPA targets rather than inventing an 86% midpoint multiplier for attribution would make the daily rules much safer to execute.

strength: The math is phenomenal—it accurately calculates 90-day break-even, builds budgets to clear the platform's learning phase, and uses the exact customer quotes for hooks.

to10: It is essentially a 10; correcting the minor misread on the trend sound's ad rights would make it completely flawless.

strength: It accurately calculates the hook costs from Meta and sets up a very clean, easy-to-read weekly budget phasing plan.

to10: Design a true geo-holdout test for incrementality, and use the exact customer verbatim quotes from the brief for the ad hooks rather than paraphrasing.

strength: Perfectly catches the hidden constraints in the data (dark scuffs and the missing front pocket) and translates them into hard creative guardrails.
mistake: None of significance; it is a masterclass in reading an e-commerce brief.

strength: Spots the wasted $24k spend on the label-reading hook and uses the historical CPA and view rate data to set exact mathematical guardrails for the test plan.

strength: Delivers very clean, ready-to-shoot scripts that strictly follow the brand guidelines and beautifully capture the natural language of the target personas.

strength: Writes punchy, on-brand copy that cleverly incorporates the actual review phrasing within strict character limits.

strength: Incredible business acumen; it calculated the historical daily spend from the raw data, set up a proper A/B test with a control, and included tracking and early cut rules.
mistake: None; it executes both the creative copywriting and the operational media buying strategy flawlessly.
